## Posterior Asymptotics And Bernstein Von Mises
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/13-graduate-statistics/1_posterior-asymptotics-and-bernstein-von-mises/

## Posterior Asymptotics and the Bernstein–von Mises Theorem

**Tier: R (Research).** Builds on measure-theoretic probability and the
undergraduate treatment of point estimation. This is where Bayesian statistics
meets asymptotic analysis, and where the question "when is the Bayesian answer
also the frequentist answer?" becomes a theorem.

## Recall prompts

Attempt these from memory before reading.

- State the weak law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.
- What is the Fisher information for an i.i.d. sample? For what class of models
  is it well defined?
- What is a prior, a posterior, and a marginal likelihood; in measure-theoretic
  terms?
- Give an estimator that is consistent but not asymptotically normal.

## Motivation: the question the theorem answers

Suppose you have data $X_1, \dots, X_n$ i.i.d. from an unknown $P_{\theta_0}$,
a prior $\Pi$ on a parameter space $\Theta$, and you compute the posterior

$$
\Pi_n(B) = \frac{\int_B \prod_i p_{\theta}(X_i)\, d\Pi(\theta)}
{\int_\Theta \prod_i p_{\theta}(X_i)\, d\Pi(\theta)}.
$$

As $n \to \infty$, two things you might hope:

1. The posterior concentrates near the truth (**consistency**).
2. The posterior looks Gaussian, centred at the maximum likelihood estimator,
   with covariance $I(\theta_0)^{-1}/n$; the same as the frequentist sampling
   distribution of the MLE (**Bernstein–von Mises**).

The second is the remarkable one. It says that after enough data, the Bayesian
uncertainty statement and the frequentist confidence statement *coincide*: a
95% credible interval is asymptotically a 95% confidence interval. That
frequentist–Bayes agreement is not automatic, and knowing exactly when it holds
and when it fails is an active research area.

## Consistency: Doob and Schwartz

**Theorem (A, Doob 1949).** If the model is identifiable and the prior
associates probability one to a set of parameters on which the posterior is
consistent, then the posterior is consistent almost surely under the prior.

Doob's theorem is nearly free but nearly circular: it holds *prior*-almost
surely, so a prior that puts mass on bad parameters is excluded by assumption.
The substantive result is Schwartz's.

**Theorem (A, Schwartz 1965).** If the true $\theta_0$ is in the support of the
prior and the model satisfies an entropy condition; for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a sieve of tests separating $\theta_0$ from the $\varepsilon$-ball
around it, with exponentially small type-II error; then the posterior
probability of $\{\theta : d(\theta, \theta_0) > \varepsilon\}$ tends to $0$.

The entropy condition is the substantive hypothesis. It is checkable, it fails
in interesting cases, and its failure is what drives most of the modern
literature.

**Worked example (U).** Bernoulli with a Beta prior. The posterior is
$\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha + n p_n,\ \beta + n(1-p_n))$, which concentrates at
$p_0$ at rate $n^{-1/2}$ for any interior prior. Consistency holds for every
$p_0 \in (0,1)$; it fails at the endpoints if the prior puts zero mass there -
the beta prior with $\alpha = \beta = 1/2$ puts unbounded density at 0 and 1,
and consistency at $p_0 = 0$ then requires care.

> **Exercise.** Show the posterior mass outside $(p_0 \pm \varepsilon)$ is
> bounded by $e^{-c n}$ for some $c > 0$, using Hoeffding's inequality on the
> likelihood ratio.

### Proofs of the consistency theorems

**Theorem (Doob, proved).** Let the model be identifiable; distinct $\theta$
give distinct laws of the infinite sequence; and let $\pi(\Theta_0) > 0$. Then
the posterior is consistent at $\pi$-almost every $\theta$: under the joint law
$\pi \otimes P_\theta^{\mathbb{N}}$, the posterior of every neighbourhood of
$\theta_0$ tends to $1$.

*Proof.* Make $\theta$ random with law $\pi$ and generate $X_1, X_2, \dots$
conditionally i.i.d. given $\theta$. For a measurable $B \subseteq \Theta$,
consider the posterior probabilities

$$
M_n = \Pi(\theta \in B \mid X_1, \dots, X_n).
$$

The tower property of conditional expectation gives
$\mathbb{E}[M_{n+1} \mid X_1, \dots, X_n] = M_n$: the $M_n$ form a **bounded
martingale**, values in $[0, 1]$. By Doob's martingale convergence theorem,
$M_n \to M_\infty$ almost surely, and the limit is the conditional expectation
of the indicator against the *full* data σ-field:

$$
M_\infty = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(\theta \in B) \mid X_1, X_2, \dots].
$$

Now the tail structure enters. Under identifiability, the exchangeable tail
σ-field of the joint law is (up to null sets) generated by $\theta$ itself, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(\theta \in B) \mid \text{tail}]
=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{on } \{\theta \in B\},\\
0 & \text{on } \{\theta \notin B\},
\end{cases}
$$

up to a $\pi$-null set. Taking $B$ through a countable base of neighbourhoods
of $\theta_0$ and intersecting the countably many almost-sure events gives
posterior concentration at $\pi$-almost every $\theta_0$. $\blacksquare$

*The catch, stated.* Doob's theorem speaks under the *joint* law: consistency
holds for prior-almost every $\theta_0$. But a $\pi$-null set can contain open
sets when the prior is not equivalent to Lebesgue-type mass on the support -
Freedman's counterexample below exploits exactly this gap. Closing it needs
control at *every* $\theta_0$, which is what Schwartz's testing condition
provides.

**Theorem (Schwartz, proved in structure).** Suppose for a neighbourhood
$\Theta_0$ of the true $\theta_0$ there are tests $\varphi_n$ of
$H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ versus $H_1: \theta \notin \Theta_0$ with exponentially
small errors:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\,\varphi_n \leq e^{-n\epsilon},
\qquad
\sup_{\theta \notin \Theta_0}\,\mathbb{E}_\theta\,(1 - \varphi_n) \leq e^{-nc},
$$

and $\pi(\Theta_0) > 0$. Then the posterior of $\Theta_0^c$ decays
exponentially: $\Pi(\Theta_0^c \mid X^{(n)}) \leq C\,e^{-n c'}$ for some
$c' > 0$.

*Proof structure.* The two test inequalities bound the likelihood ratio: on
$\Theta_0^c$, the average likelihood is at most $e^{-nc}$ times what $H_0$
predicts, and on the event where the test rejects, the same holds pointwise.
Since $\pi(\Theta_0) > 0$, the marginal likelihood over $\Theta_0$ is at least
$\pi(\Theta_0)\,p_{\theta_0}(X^{(n)})$, and on the test's *acceptance* event
the likelihood under any $\theta \in \Theta_0^c$ is at most $e^{-nc}$ times the
likelihood at $\theta_0$ up to the exponentially small type-I error. Combining:

$$
\Pi(\Theta_0^c \mid X^{(n)})
\leq \frac{e^{-nc}}{\pi(\Theta_0)} + \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi_n\text{-terms}
\leq \frac{2\,e^{-n c'}}{\pi(\Theta_0)},
$$

for $c'$ the smaller of $c$ and $\epsilon$ up to constants; exponential decay
in $n$. $\blacksquare$

*What the structure teaches.* Every hypothesis of the nonparametric
contraction theorem above replaces one move of this proof. The exponential
testing condition is Schwartz's hypothesis verbatim; the sieve is what
replaces the compact complement $\Theta_0^c$ when entropy is infinite; and the
prior-mass condition is the Kullback–Leibler property. Each of the three moves: exponential testing, entropy control, prior mass – is a hypothesis in the
modern theorem, and each fails in a way the failure-mode section below
documents.

## Posterior contraction rates

Consistency is qualitative. The quantitative question is: how fast?

**Definition.** A sequence $\varepsilon_n \to 0$ is a **contraction rate** if

$$
\Pi_n\left(\theta : d(\theta, \theta_0) > M_n \varepsilon_n \mid X\right) \to 0
$$

for every $M_n \to \infty$.

**Theorem (A, Ghosal–Ghosh–van der Vaart).** Under conditions on the prior's
mass near the truth (a *prior mass condition*) and on the complexity of the
model (entropy with bracketing), the posterior contracts at rate

$$
\varepsilon_n \asymp n^{-\frac{\beta}{2\beta + 1}}
$$

for a $\beta$-smooth true density in a nonparametric model.

That rate is the minimax rate; the Bayesian procedure is rate-optimal, which
is far from obvious for a procedure defined by a prior rather than an
optimisation.

**Worked example (A).** Gaussian white noise observations
$dY(t) = f(t)\,dt + n^{-1/2}\,dW(t)$ with a Gaussian prior on $f$ in a Sobolev
ball $H^\beta$. The posterior contracts at $n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}$, matching
the minimax rate; and the *shape* of the posterior is then shown by
Szabó, van der Vaart and van Zanten (2015) to be *not* Bernstein–von Mises: the
credible sets are not honest confidence sets. Rate optimality and honesty come
apart, and that separation is the modern research frontier.

## The Bernstein–von Mises phenomenon

**Theorem (A, van der Vaart 1998, Ch. 10; Le Cam).** Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be open, $p_\theta$ smooth in $\theta$ near $\theta_0$, the
Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$ positive definite, the prior positive and
continuous at $\theta_0$, and the model otherwise regular. Then for almost
every sequence $X_1, X_2, \dots$,

$$
\sup_{h}\left| \Pi_n\left(\sqrt{n}(\theta - \hat\theta_n) \le h \mid X\right)
- \Phi_{I(\theta_0)^{-1}}(h) \right| \xrightarrow{P} 0,
$$

where $\hat\theta_n$ is any consistent estimator sequence.

**In words.** The posterior, shifted and rescaled, converges to a Gaussian
centred at the MLE with covariance $I(\theta_0)^{-1}/n$; the frequentist
limit law.

**Worked example (U).** The Bernoulli model with a flat prior. The posterior is
$\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha + \sum x_i, \beta + n - \sum x_i)$, which for large $n$
is approximately $\mathcal{N}(\hat p, \hat p(1-\hat p)/n)$; exactly the
CLT-based sampling distribution of $\hat p$. The theorem says this is generic,
not a coincidence of the Beta family.

**Why it matters for practice.** Under BvM, Laplace's approximation to the
posterior is asymptotically exact, MCMC on a well-behaved posterior gives
frequentist-valid intervals, and the choice of prior is asymptotically
irrelevant at rate $n^{-1/2}$. That last claim is the load-bearing one for
objective Bayes, and it is exactly what fails below.

## Where Bernstein–von Mises fails

This is the research content. Each failure is an active area.

**Nonparametric models.** As above: Gaussian priors in white noise contract at
the right rate but the posterior shape is wrong. Freedman (1999) showed the
posterior in a nonparametric normal-means problem can be inconsistent in
shape even while concentrating. Cox (1993) and Diaconis–Freedman (1986) gave
earlier examples. The resolution; priors adapted to the truth's smoothness, or
honest adaptive credible sets (Szabó, van der Vaart & van Zanten; Bull; Nickl &
Szabó); is a substantial modern literature.

**Model misspecification.** If the true distribution is not in the model, the
posterior concentrates on the *KL minimiser* and BvM holds with the sandwich
information $I_1 I_0^{-1} I_1$ rather than $I_0$; Kleijn and van der Vaart
(2012). The Bayesian answer then matches the *sandwich* frequentist answer, not
the model-based one.

**Separation and irregular identification.** In mixture models and other
singularly identifiable models, the Fisher information can be singular and BvM
fails in a strong sense. Posterior contraction can be slower than any
polynomial rate; recent work (e.g. on deconvolution and mixture proportions)
quantifies exactly how much slower.

**High dimension.** If $k = k_n$ grows with $n$, BvM holds only for
$k_n^5/n \to 0$ (Bickel & Kleijn) in smooth models, and in sparse models the
posterior can be very far from Gaussian. The interplay between sparsity,
priors and BvM is the current frontier.

**Prior dependence at rate $n^{-1/2}$.** BvM says the prior is irrelevant *at
the first order*. At the second order it is not, and that matters for
computation, for credible set calibration, and for the behaviour of MCMC.

## Proof of the Bernstein–von Mises theorem

The proof is worth reading because its machinery; local asymptotic normality,
contiguity; is the same machinery every modern result in this area is proved
with: contraction rates, the misspecified version below, and the
high-dimensional $k_n^5/n \to 0$ condition are all proved by running the same
argument with harder estimates inside it.

Write it in one dimension. The $k$-dimensional case is identical with
$I(\theta_0)$ a matrix and $\Delta_n$ a vector; only the notation is heavier.

**Step 1: local asymptotic normality.** Reparametrise to the *local* parameter
$h = \sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0)$ and expand the log-likelihood ratio about
$\theta_0$:

$$
\log\frac{p_{\theta_0 + h/\sqrt{n}}^{(n)}(X)}{p_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(X)}
= \frac{h}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \dot\ell_{\theta_0}(X_i)
- \frac{h^2}{2} I(\theta_0) + R_n,
$$

where $\dot\ell_\theta = \partial_\theta \log p_\theta$ and $R_n \to 0$ in
probability, uniformly in $h$ in compacts. This is the LAN condition. The two
main terms are the *score at scale* $\Delta_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_i \dot\ell_{\theta_0}(X_i)$ and a deterministic quadratic penalty $-h^2 I/2$.
Smoothness of $p_\theta$ and finiteness of $I(\theta_0)$ give it by Taylor's
theorem; the content of the hypothesis "regular model" is that $R_n$ is
controlled.

**Step 2: what LAN says about the likelihood ratio.** Define

$$
Z_{n,h} = \frac{p_{\theta_0 + h/\sqrt{n}}^{(n)}(X)}{p_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(X)}.
$$

By Step 1, $Z_{n,h} = \exp(h\Delta_n - \tfrac{1}{2}h^2 I + R_n)$. Under
$P_{\theta_0}$, $\Delta_n \Rightarrow N(0, I)$ by the ordinary CLT, and the
map $h \mapsto Z_{n,h}$ is asymptotically the *likelihood ratio of a Gaussian
shift experiment*: an experiment in which one observes $\Delta = h + \text{noise}$
with $\text{noise} \sim N(0, I)$. That is what "local asymptotic normality"
means, and it is why the normal shows up on both sides of the theorem.

**Step 3: rewrite the posterior in the local parameter.** The posterior density
of $h$ given $X$, at the true $\theta_0$, is proportional to

$$
\pi\!\left(\theta_0 + \frac{h}{\sqrt n}\right)
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\,p_{\theta_0 + h/\sqrt n}^{(n)}(X),
$$

and dividing through by the value at $h = 0$ turns it into

$$
\frac{\pi(\theta_0 + h/\sqrt n)}{\pi(\theta_0)} \cdot Z_{n,h}.
$$

Both factors are now under control: the prior factor is bounded, and tends to
$1$ uniformly on compacts by continuity of $\pi$ at $\theta_0$; and $Z_{n,h}$ is
the LAN expression from Step 2. This is the whole reason the theorem needs the
prior to be *positive and continuous at $\theta_0$*; positivity keeps the
normalising constant from vanishing, and continuity makes the prior factor
asymptotically constant, which is exactly the sense in which the prior drops out.

**Step 4: the main estimate.** One shows that for every $\varepsilon > 0$,

$$
\int_{|h| > \varepsilon\sqrt n}
\frac{\pi(\theta_0 + h/\sqrt n)}{\pi(\theta_0)}
Z_{n,h} \, dh \xrightarrow{P} 0.
$$

This is the *only* genuinely hard estimate in the proof, and it is where
consistency is spent. Outside a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ the likelihood ratio
decays exponentially, by Schwartz's test condition; the same condition that
gave posterior consistency in the section above. The theorem is not independent
of consistency; it is consistency plus a local Gaussian approximation.

**Step 5: the characteristic function.** For the *total variation* statement
claimed, it suffices to prove convergence of characteristic functions on the
local parameter, since the tails are already handled in Step 4. For
$t \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.e^{itH_n}\right| X\right]
= \frac{\displaystyle\int e^{ith} Z_{n,h}\,dh}
{\displaystyle\int Z_{n,h}\,dh}
\qquad \text{with } H_n = \sqrt n(\theta - \theta_0),
$$

and substituting the LAN form of $Z_{n,h}$:

$$
= \frac{\displaystyle\int e^{ith}\,
e^{h\Delta_n - h^2 I/2}\,dh}
{\displaystyle\int e^{h\Delta_n - h^2 I/2}\,dh}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\frac{\displaystyle\int e^{ith}\,e^{-I(h - \Delta/I)^2/2}\,dh}
{\displaystyle\int e^{-I(h-\Delta/I)^2/2}\,dh}
= e^{it\Delta/I}\, e^{-t^2/(4I)},
$$

the characteristic function of $N(\Delta/I, 1/(2I))$. Since
$\Delta_n/I \Rightarrow N(0, 1/I)$ under $P_{\theta_0}$, and the credible
interval endpoints are continuous functionals of this Gaussian, the rescaled
posterior converges in distribution; and by the usual lifting from weak to
total variation for measures with densities bounded as in Step 4, in total
variation:

$$
\sup_h \left| \Pi_n\big(h \le \sqrt n(\theta-\theta_0) \mid X\big) - \Phi_{1/I}(h) \right| \xrightarrow{P} 0.
$$

Replace $1/I$ by $I(\theta_0)^{-1}$ and $\theta_0$ by any consistent
$\hat\theta_n$ to get the stated form. $\blacksquare$

**What each hypothesis bought.** Smoothness and finite information gave LAN in
Step 1. Prior continuity made the prior drop out in Step 3. Positivity of the
prior kept the denominator alive. Schwartz's conditions did the work in Step 4,
which is why the theorem is stated for a *consistent* model: BvM is not an
addition to consistency but a refinement of it. And contiguity; the only tool
not yet named; is what licenses transferring statements between
$P_{\theta_0+h/\sqrt n}$ and $P_{\theta_0}$, which is what makes the local
argument legitimate.

## Counterexamples

**Freedman's theorem.** There exist priors with full support for which the
posterior is inconsistent at every parameter in the support. Full support is
therefore *not* enough for consistency; the Schwartz conditions are doing real
work.

**BvM without consistency.** The posterior can concentrate at a wrong point and
still be asymptotically Gaussian around it. Consistency and asymptotic
normality are separate properties.

**Diaconis–Freedman.** In a finite mixture of normals, the posterior on the
mixture weights can fail to concentrate at any rate, because the likelihood is
unbounded and the parameter space is not locally identifiable.

  Schwartz's.
- What is a contraction rate? State the rate for a $\beta$-smooth density under
  a Gaussian prior.
- State the Bernstein–von Mises theorem and its hypotheses.
- Give three settings in which BvM fails.
- Why does the frequentist–Bayes agreement in BvM not settle the debate about
  priors?

## Interleaving problems

1. (Measure theory.) Show the posterior is a regular conditional distribution of
   $\theta$ given $X_1, \dots, X_n$ under the joint law $\theta \sim \Pi$,
   $X_i | \theta \sim P_\theta$.
2. (Real analysis.) Prove the Laplace approximation
   $\int e^{-n f(\theta)} d\theta \approx e^{-n f(\hat\theta)} \sqrt{2\pi/(n f''(\hat\theta))}$ and identify where regularity is used.
3. (Probability.) Show that for the Bernoulli model the posterior variance is
   $\hat p (1 - \hat p)/(n + \alpha + \beta)$, and compare to the Cramér–Rao
   bound.
4. (Functional analysis.) In the white noise model, show the eigenvalues of the
   covariance operator of the Gaussian prior on $H^\beta$ decay as $j^{-2\beta}$,
   and connect that to the contraction rate.
5. (Decision theory.) Under squared-error loss show the Bayes estimator is the
   posterior mean, and under BvM show it agrees with the MLE to order
   $O(n^{-1})$.

## Posterior Contraction Rates
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/13-graduate-statistics/2_posterior-contraction-rates/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "mathematics", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "13 Graduate Statistics", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/13-graduate-statistics"}, {"name": "2_posterior-contraction-rates", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/13-graduate-statistics/2_posterior-contraction-rates"}]
}
</script>

Consistency says the posterior converges; contraction rates say how fast. The
distinction is not cosmetic; a consistency theorem that permits convergence at
any rate is compatible with the estimate being useless for prediction, and the
rate is what a practitioner needs to plan a study. The contraction-rate theory
is also where nonparametric Bayes earns its keep: the parametric rate
$n^{-1/2}$ is a ceiling that nonparametric models cannot reach, and the
achieved rate depends on the smoothness of the truth and the flexibility of the
prior in a way that the theorem makes precise.

The prerequisite is the [Bernstein–von Mises
page](/13-graduate-statistics/1_posterior-asymptotics-and-bernstein-von-mises/):
the contraction proof there (Step 4's tail estimate) is exactly the mechanism
generalised here, with sieves replacing compact sets and entropy replacing
finiteness.

## Intuition

Picture the posterior as a cloud of uncertainty around the true parameter. In a
parametric model; one unknown number; the cloud shrinks like $n^{-1/2}$: ten
times the data, three times the precision. In a nonparametric model; an
unknown *function*; the cloud must shrink in every direction simultaneously,
and the rate depends on how many "directions" the function space has at the
truth's smoothness. A twice-differentiable function lives in a space of
effective dimension $(2\beta + 1)/\beta$ per unit of smoothness $\beta$; the
minimax rate $n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}$ is what that effective dimension buys.

The prior's job is to place enough mass near the truth for the posterior to
find it, and to not place so much mass on overly complex functions that the
posterior chases noise. Both conditions are formalised below; the prior mass
condition and the entropy condition; and neither is optional.

## 1. The definition

**Definition.** Let $d$ be a metric on the parameter space. A sequence
$\varepsilon_n \to 0$ (with $n\varepsilon_n^2 \to \infty$) is a **contraction
rate** at $\theta_0$ if, for every $M_n \to \infty$,

$$
\Pi_n\!\left(\theta : d(\theta, \theta_0) > M_n \varepsilon_n \;\middle|\; X^{(n)}\right) \xrightarrow{P_{\theta_0}} 0.
$$

The $M_n \to \infty$ factor means the posterior puts vanishing mass outside a
band that is $M_n$ times the rate wide; so the rate is the *scale* of the
posterior's spread, not a hard boundary.

**Why $n\varepsilon_n^2 \to \infty$.** The contraction proof needs the
information to grow faster than the rate shrinks; without that, the posterior
could concentrate at rate $\varepsilon_n$ while the evidence is still too weak
to distinguish $\theta_0$ from its neighbourhood. For parametric models,
$\varepsilon_n = n^{-1/2}$ gives $n\varepsilon_n^2 = 1$; the boundary case,
which is why the parametric rate is the fastest possible at this level of
generality.

## 2. The two conditions

**Definition (prior mass condition).** The prior puts at least
$e^{-n\epsilon^2}$ mass on an $\varepsilon_n$-ball around the truth:

$$
\Pi\big(\theta : d(\theta, \theta_0) \leq \varepsilon_n\big) \geq e^{-n\epsilon^2}
\quad\text{for some } \epsilon < \varepsilon_n.
$$

**Definition (entropy condition).** For every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a
set of $\mathcal{F}$-brackets covering the model's $\epsilon$-ball around
$\theta_0$ with logarithmic bracketing entropy
$H(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, d) \leq n\epsilon^2$; the number of brackets grows
at most exponentially in $n\epsilon^2$.

**Theorem (Ghosal–Ghosh–van der Vaart, structure).** If both conditions hold at
rate $\varepsilon_n$, then the posterior contracts at rate $\varepsilon_n$: for
every $M_n \to \infty$,

$$
\Pi_n\big(d(\theta, \theta_0) > M_n\varepsilon_n \mid X^{(n)}\big) \xrightarrow{P_{\theta_0}} 0.
$$

*Proof structure.* The proof is a generalisation of [the Bernstein–von Mises
page's Step 4](/13-graduate-statistics/1_posterior-asymptotics-and-bernstein-von-mises/):
the prior mass condition provides the lower bound on the denominator (the
marginal likelihood over the $\varepsilon_n$-ball), and the entropy condition
provides the upper bound on the numerator (the posterior mass outside it) via a
testing argument over the bracketing set. The testing step replaces the finite
compact of the parametric case with a finite bracketing cover of the infinite-
dimensional model, and the entropy bound is what makes the cover finite. The
exponent $n\epsilon_n^2$ appears in both conditions; it is the information
budget, and the rate is the largest $\varepsilon_n$ at which both conditions
can hold simultaneously. $\blacksquare$

**The minimax rate for $\beta$-smooth densities.** For a $\beta$-Hölder true
density on $[0,1]$, the optimal rate is

$$
\varepsilon_n \asymp n^{-\frac{\beta}{2\beta + 1}},
$$

achieved by priors whose smoothness matches $\beta$ (spline priors, Gaussian
process priors with matched length-scale). The rate degrades as $\beta$
decreases; rougher truths are harder to estimate; and saturates at
$n^{-1/2}$ as $\beta \to \infty$, recovering the parametric rate.

## 3. Why nonparametric is harder

The parametric rate $n^{-1/2}$ requires $O(1)$ parameters; the nonparametric
rate for $\beta$-smooth functions requires the *effective dimension* of the
function class at scale $\varepsilon_n$ to be $O(\varepsilon_n^{-1/\beta})$.
The prior must place its mass on that limited-dimensional subspace; which is
what the entropy condition formalises; and if the prior spreads its mass over
too many directions, the posterior chases noise instead of signal.

**Freedman's counterexample, located.** The [frontier
page](/13-graduate-statistics/1_posterior-asymptotics-and-bernstein-von-mises/)
notes Freedman (1999) showed the posterior can be inconsistent in shape even
while concentrating. The mechanism is the prior mass condition failing *in
shape*: the prior places mass near the truth in $L^1$ but not in the directions
that distinguish the truth from its neighbours, so the posterior concentrates
but its credible intervals under-cover. The prior mass condition is necessary
but not sufficient; the shape of the mass matters.

## 4. Where the frontier is

The nonparametric contraction theory is complete for the models it covers:
Gaussian-process priors with matched length-scale, spline priors, Pólya-tree
priors for densities. The open questions are at the boundaries:

- **Adaptation.** A prior that achieves the optimal rate without knowing
  $\beta$ in advance. Hierarchical priors put a hyperprior on the smoothness;
  the theory shows this works for some hyperpriors and fails for others
  (impossibility results by Hoffmann and Nickl mark exactly where adaptation is
  free and where it must be paid for).
- **Deep priors.** Neural-network priors on functions: their approximation
  theory is known, their posterior contraction theory is being written now.
- **Structured nonparametrics.** Contractions on function spaces with
  constraints (monotonicity, log-concavity); the constraint changes the
  entropy and hence the rate, and the theory is model-specific.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Quoting a contraction rate without its conditions.** Both the prior mass
  and entropy conditions are needed; either alone is insufficient, and each
  fails differently.
- **Assuming $n^{-1/2}$ universally.** The parametric rate is a ceiling; the
  nonparametric rate depends on smoothness and is always at best
  $n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}$ for finite $\beta$.
- **Reading "contraction" as "consistency".** Contraction is consistency plus a
  rate; a rate theorem without consistency is vacuous, and consistency without
  a rate is uninformative.
- **Using the Bernstein–von Mises theorem in nonparametric models.** BvM *fails*
  in infinite dimensions for Gaussian priors (Freedman 1999): the posterior
  shape is wrong even when the contraction rate is right. The credible
  intervals from a nonparametric posterior are not automatically
  frequentist-valid; that requires shape-matched priors or Bernstein–von Mises
  for adaptive priors, both open research areas.
- **Assuming the prior mass condition holds because the prior has full
  support.** Full support means every open set has positive prior mass; the
  condition needs that mass to be at least $e^{-n\epsilon^2}$; exponentially
  small is not zero, but the *rate* at which the mass decays matters, and full
  support alone gives no rate.

## Cross-References

- **[Posterior Asymptotics and the Bernstein–von Mises Theorem](/13-graduate-statistics/1_posterior-asymptotics-and-bernstein-von-mises/)**; the parametric ancestor of this theory, and the proof whose Step 4 generalises here.
- **[Measure Theory](https://mathematics.wyattau.com/10-measure-theory/)**; the $L^p$ spaces and covering-number machinery behind the entropy condition.
- **[Sobolev Spaces](/11-functional-analysis/10_sobolev-spaces/)**; the smoothness scale in which the rate $\beta$ is measured.
- **[Gaussian Processes](https://machine-learning.wyattau.com/1-probabilistic-machine-learning/9_gaussian-processes/)**; the prior class whose contraction theory is the most developed.
- **[Statistical Decision Theory](https://machine-learning.wyattau.com/1-probabilistic-machine-learning/2_statistical-decision-theory/)**; the loss framework in which the minimax rate is defined.
- [The Research Frontier](/13-graduate-statistics/1_posterior-asymptotics-and-bernstein-von-mises/); where this theory meets its open questions.

## Ito Integration And Formula
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/14-graduate-stochastic-analysis/1_ito-integration-and-formula/

## Stochastic Calculus: Itô Integration and the Itô Formula

**Tier: R (Research).** Builds on probability spaces, measure theory, real
analysis and functional analysis. The subject is the mathematics of randomness
that changes in time, and it is the language of mathematical finance, stochastic
PDEs, and the modern theory of regularity for rough functions.

## Recall prompts

Attempt these from memory *before* reading.

- What is a filtration? What does it mean for a process to be adapted?
- State the three properties that define Brownian motion.
- What is the quadratic variation of a function, and what is it for a
  differentiable function?
- State the ordinary chain rule.
- What does the Lebesgue integral of a function against a measure of unbounded
  variation require?

## Motivation: the ordinary integral cannot be used

You want to model a stock price, a diffusing particle, or a noisy signal. The
natural object is an integral

$$
\int_0^t \sigma(s)\, dW(s)
$$

where $W$ is Brownian motion; the integral of a strategy against a random
noise. The problem is that $dW(s)$ is not a measure. Brownian paths have
unbounded variation on every interval, so the Riemann–Stieltjes integral does
not exist: the sums do not converge no matter how you partition.

That is not a technicality. It is the mathematical statement that the noise is
*rough*, and roughness is the whole point. The Itô integral is the repair, and
the repair has a price: the chain rule acquires an extra term, and that term is
what makes stochastic calculus a different subject from ordinary calculus.

## Brownian motion

**Definition (F, in this subject).** A standard Brownian motion $W$ is a
process with:

1. $W_0 = 0$ almost surely.
2. Independent increments: $W_{t} - W_{s}$ is independent of the past for
   $s < t$.
3. Gaussian increments: $W_t - W_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t-s)$.
4. Continuous paths.

**Three properties worth knowing by heart.**

<div class="table-wrap">

| Property | Statement | Why it matters |
| -------- | --------- | -------------- |
| Almost sure nowhere differentiability | Paley–Wiener–Zygmund | there is no $dW/dt$ as a function |
| Quadratic variation $[W]_t = t$ | almost surely | the source of the extra term in Itô's formula |
| Scaling: $W_{ct} \sim \sqrt{c}\,W_t$ | in distribution | Brownian motion is its own coarse-grained limit |

</div>

The quadratic variation is the central object. For a differentiable function
$f$, the sums $\sum (f(t_{i+1}) - f(t_i))^2$ over a partition tend to $0$ like
the mesh. For Brownian motion they tend to $t$; a *positive, finite, non-random
limit*. Brownian motion accumulates exactly $t$ worth of roughness, and that is
a deterministic fact about almost every path.

## Why the Itô integral cannot be a Riemann–Stieltjes integral

For a deterministic integrand $f$ and an integrator $g$ of bounded variation,
the Riemann–Stieltjes sums $\sum f(\xi_i)(g(t_{i+1}) - g(t_i))$ converge
regardless of where the evaluation point $\xi_i$ sits in $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$.

For Brownian motion, the choice of $\xi_i$ changes the answer. Taking $\xi_i$
at the left endpoint gives one limit; taking it at the midpoint gives a
*different* limit; the difference is exactly half the quadratic variation of
the cross term.

So there is no integral free of that choice. Itô's choice is the **left
endpoint**, which has a probabilistic meaning: $\xi_i$ is then known given the
past, so the integrand is *non-anticipating*. That is what makes the integral
adapted, and adaptedness is what makes it a martingale; the property that does
all the work.

**The price and the payoff.** The Itô integral is not a pathwise object; it is
defined as an $L^2$ limit. It has no meaning for a fixed realisation of $W$. In
exchange it is a martingale with

$$
E\left[\left(\int_0^t \sigma\, dW\right)^2\right] = E\left[\int_0^t \sigma^2\, ds\right],
$$

which is the Itô isometry, and it is what makes the integral usable.

## The Itô formula

**Theorem (R, Itô 1944).** Let $X_t$ satisfy $dX_t = \mu_t\,dt + \sigma_t\,dW_t$
and let $f$ be twice continuously differentiable. Then

$$
df(X_t) = f'(X_t)\,dX_t + \frac{1}{2} f''(X_t)\, d\langle X\rangle_t,
$$

and for Brownian motion $d\langle W \rangle_t = dt$, so

$$
df(W_t) = f'(W_t)\,dW_t + \frac{1}{2} f''(W_t)\,dt.
$$

**Where the extra term comes from.** Taylor-expand $f(X_t)$ to second order:

$$
df = f'\,dX + \frac{1}{2} f''\,(dX)^2.
$$

In ordinary calculus $(dX)^2$ is $o(dX)$ and vanishes. For Brownian motion,
$(dW)^2$ is *exactly* $dt$; that is the statement $[W]_t = t$. The second-order
term is of the same order as the first, so it cannot be dropped.

**Worked example (R, in full).** Find the SDE for $Y_t = W_t^2$.

Take $f(x) = x^2$. Then $f'(x) = 2x$ and $f''(x) = 2$, so

$$
d(W_t^2) = 2W_t\,dW_t + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\,dt = 2W_t\,dW_t + dt.
$$

Rearranging, $W_t^2 - t = \int_0^t 2W_s\,dW_s$, which shows directly that the
Itô integral is a martingale: $W_t^2 - t$ has zero drift. In ordinary calculus
you would get $d(W^2) = 2W\,dW$ and no $dt$ term; the $dt$ is the Itô
correction, and it is the quadratic variation appearing.

**Worked example (R, geometric Brownian motion).** Financial models use

$$
dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t.
$$

Find $d(\log S_t)$. With $f(x) = \log x$, $f'(x) = 1/x$, $f''(x) = -1/x^2$:

$$
d(\log S_t) = \frac{1}{S_t}\,dS_t - \frac{1}{2S_t^2}\,\sigma^2 S_t^2\,dt
= \left(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)dt + \sigma\,dW_t.
$$

So $\log S_t = \log S_0 + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t$, and $S_t$ is
log-normal with *drift $\mu - \sigma^2/2$*, not $\mu$. Missing the $-\sigma^2/2$
is the most common error in the subject, and it comes precisely from dropping
the Itô term.

## Proofs

Three proofs. The first establishes the isometry, which is the integral's
definition; the second establishes quadratic variation, which the Itô formula
assumes; the third is the formula itself. The order matters, because the third
uses the second and would be circular without it.

**Theorem 1 (Itô isometry).** For simple $\sigma$,
$\left\|\int_0^t \sigma\,dW\right\|_2^2 = \mathbb{E}\int_0^t \sigma^2\,ds$, and
the simple adapted maps are dense in $L^2(\Omega \times [0,t])$, so the isometry
extends the integral to all of $L^2$.

*Proof.* Let $\sigma_t = \sigma_{t_i}$ on $(t_i, t_{i+1}]$ and
$\Delta W_i = W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i}$. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\Big(\sum_i \sigma_{t_i}\Delta W_i\Big)^{\!2}
= \sum_i \mathbb{E}\big[\sigma_{t_i}^2 \Delta W_i^2\big]
+ 2\sum_{i<j} \mathbb{E}\big[\sigma_{t_i}\sigma_{t_j}\Delta W_i \Delta W_j\big].
$$

For a cross term, condition on $\mathcal{F}_{t_j}$: $\sigma_{t_j}$ and $\Delta W_i$
for $i<j$ are $\mathcal{F}_{t_j}$-measurable, and
$\mathbb{E}[\Delta W_j \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_j}] = 0$ by independent increments, so
the term is zero. For the diagonal,
$\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{t_i}^2\Delta W_i^2] = \mathbb{E}[\sigma_{t_i}^2](t_{i+1}-t_i)$
by the same conditioning. Summing gives the isometry.

Simple adapted processes are dense in $L^2(\Omega\times[0,t])$, and because the
map is an isometry on them it is $L^2$-continuous, so it extends uniquely to the
closure. That extension *is* the Itô integral: an $L^2$ object, defined by
continuity rather than pathwise. The cross terms did not merely come out small --
they vanished because of adaptedness, the same property that fixed the choice of
left endpoint above. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem 2 (quadratic variation of Brownian motion).** For partitions with mesh
$\to 0$,

$$
\sum_i (W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i})^2 \xrightarrow{L^2} t.
$$

*Proof.* Write $Q_n$ for the sum and $\Delta t_i = t_{i+1}-t_i$. Then
$\mathbb{E}Q_n = \sum_i \Delta t_i = t$, so it is enough to show the variance
vanishes. The increments are independent, and $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i^2) = 2(\Delta t_i)^2$ for a Gaussian, so

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Q_n) = \sum_i 2(\Delta t_i)^2
\leq 2 \max_i \Delta t_i \sum_i \Delta t_i = 2t\,\max_i \Delta t_i \to 0.
$$

$\blacksquare$

The single line $\sum 2(\Delta t_i)^2 \le 2t\max_i\Delta t_i$ is the entire
proof, and it is worth pausing on: quadratic variation is a *limit*, not an
identity, and for any finite partition $Q_n$ has mean $t$ but fluctuates. The
shorthand $(dW)^2 = dt$ is a statement about this $L^2$ limit, exactly as true
and exactly as informal as that.

**Theorem 3 (Itô's formula).** For $f \in C^2(\mathbb{R})$,

$$
f(W_t) = f(0) + \int_0^t f'(W_s)\,dW_s + \frac{1}{2}\int_0^t f''(W_s)\,ds.
$$

*Proof.* Partition $[0,t]$ and Taylor-expand about $W_{t_i}$:

$$
f(W_{t_{i+1}}) - f(W_{t_i})
= f'(W_{t_i})\Delta W_i + \tfrac12 f''(W_{t_i})(\Delta W_i)^2 + R_i,
$$

with $R_i = \tfrac12 (f''(\xi_i) - f''(W_{t_i}))(\Delta W_i)^2$. Summing,

$$
f(W_t) - f(0) = \sum_i f'(W_{t_i})\Delta W_i
+ \tfrac12\sum_i f''(W_{t_i})\Delta t_i
+ \tfrac12\sum_i f''(W_{t_i})\big[(\Delta W_i)^2 - \Delta t_i\big]
+ \sum_i R_i.
$$

Term by term. The first converges in $L^2$ to the Itô integral, by Theorem 1.
The second is an ordinary Riemann sum, converging to $\tfrac12\int_0^t f''\,ds$.
The third is the term Riemann-Stieltjes theory does not have, and it vanishes
*because* of Theorem 2: by Cauchy-Schwarz in $L^2$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\Big(\sum_i f''(W_{t_i})\big[(\Delta W_i)^2 - \Delta t_i\big]\Big)^{\!2}
\leq \|f''\|_\infty^2\; \mathbb{E}\Big(\sum_i \big[(\Delta W_i)^2-\Delta t_i\big]\Big)^{\!2}
\to 0.
$$

For the remainder, $f''$ is uniformly continuous, so
$\max_i|f''(\xi_i) - f''(W_{t_i})| \to 0$ in probability while
$\sum_i(\Delta W_i)^2$ is $O_P(1)$ by Theorem 2; hence
$\sum_i R_i \to 0$ in probability. $\blacksquare$

The proof explains the formula rather than merely verifying it. The extra term is
not a correction that happens to be needed: it is the second-order Taylor term
failing to be negligible, and the reason it fails is that $\sum(\Delta W_i)^2$
has a nonzero limit. For a bounded-variation integrator that sum tends to zero,
which is why ordinary calculus has no such term. Itô's formula is Taylor's
theorem with a different answer to the question "how large is $(\Delta X)^2$" --
and the answer is a property of the *integrator*, not of $f$.

## Counterexamples

<div class="table-wrap">

| Claim | True? | Counterexample |
| ----- | ----- | -------------- |
| $d(W^2) = 2W\,dW$ | no | the $+dt$ term is the quadratic variation |
| Brownian paths are differentiable | no | unbounded variation on every interval |
| The Itô integral is pathwise defined | no | it is an $L^2$ limit over all paths |
| Change of variables works as in ordinary calculus | no | the second-order term survives |
| The Stratonovich and Itô integrals agree | no | they differ by half the quadratic variation of the cross term |

</div>

The last row is the research-level content. The **Stratonovich** integral uses
the midpoint evaluation point instead of the left endpoint. It agrees with
ordinary calculus ($d(W^2) = 2W \circ dW$, no correction term), but it is not a
martingale. Itô is the natural choice for *predicting* (left endpoint = no
foresight); Stratonovich is the natural choice for *modelling physics*
(invariant under coordinate changes). The conversion between them is explicit,
and choosing the wrong one silently changes the drift.

## Where the research frontier is

- **Rough paths.** Lyons' theory constructs the integral for *any* rough signal: not just Brownian motion – by treating the iterated integrals as extra data.
  It removes the probabilistic structure entirely and gives pathwise meaning to
  what Itô defines in $L^2$. It also explains *why* Itô's correction exists: it
  is the Lévy area.
- **Malliavin calculus.** A differential calculus on Wiener space, giving
  probabilistic proofs of Hörmander's hypoellipticity theorem and a way to
  compute sensitivities of expectations with respect to the noise.
- **Stochastic PDEs.** The stochastic heat, wave and Navier–Stokes equations.
  Regularity structures (Hairer, Fields Medal 2014) extended rough paths to
  give a meaning to SPDEs whose nonlinearity is more singular than the noise.
- **Regularisation by noise.** An ODE with irregular drift that has no solution
  classically can acquire a unique one when noise is added; noise creating
  regularity rather than destroying it.

### More counterexamples

<div class="table-wrap">

| Object | Looks like | Is actually |
| ------ | ---------- | ----------- |
| $dW/dt$ | a derivative | does not exist; white noise is a distribution |
| $[W]_t$ | converges to 0 like differentiable functions | converges to $t$ |
| Itô integral for fixed $W$ | a pathwise Riemann integral | an $L^2$ limit over the probability space |
| Stratonovich integral | the same as Itô | differs by half the cross quadratic variation |

</div>

## Stochastic Pdes And Regularity Structures
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/14-graduate-stochastic-analysis/2_stochastic-pdes-and-regularity-structures/

## Stochastic PDEs: Multiplicative Noise and Regularity Structures

**Tier: R (Research).** Builds on [Itô
Integration](/14-graduate-stochastic-analysis/1_ito-integration-and-formula/),
[Measure Theory](/10-measure-theory/2_measures/), [Functional
Analysis](/11-functional-analysis/1_normed-spaces-and-banach-spaces/) and real
analysis.

## Recall prompts

Attempt these from memory *before* reading.

- What is the stochastic heat equation? Write it down.
- What does it mean for a PDE to have a solution *as a random variable*?
- Why does the deterministic parabolic theory not transfer to the stochastic case?
- State the Wick (Wiener–Itô) product. What does $dW\,dW$ equal, and how does
  that differ from $dW\,dt$?
- What is the KPZ equation, and why is it harder than the stochastic heat
  equation?

Check your answers against the text. Prompt 4 is the one the whole subject
turns on: a rule that is wrong in ordinary calculus is exactly right here.

## Motivation: a PDE whose answer is random

Ordinary PDEs are deterministic. Given a forcing term you get one solution.
Replace the forcing with Brownian motion and the question becomes strange: the
"solution" is now a random field, and asking for it means deciding what kind of
object it is, in which function space it lives, and what it means for that
object to solve the equation.

The canonical example is the **stochastic heat equation** (in physics, the
parabolic Anderson model):

$$
\partial_t u = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\partial_x^2 u + \xi\, u,
$$

where $\xi$ is space-time white noise and $u$ is the unknown. The
multiplicative term is what makes it hard: the coefficient of the highest
derivative is not a fixed constant but a random function, so the operator's
symbol fluctuates and the usual energy estimates have nothing to hold on to.

**The naive reaction is wrong.** Someone who has just learned Itô's formula
tries the deterministic route: integrate by parts, estimate the energy, hope
for the best. The estimate fails, because the constant in the estimate is
$\|\xi\|_\infty$, and space-time white noise is in no $L^p$ space at all. This
is not a technical annoyance. It means the deterministic proof has no valid
input, and a genuinely different theory is required.

## The mechanism: how noise squares

**In words.** Ordinary calculus says $dx\,dx = 0$; infinitesimals shrink
faster than they accumulate. Itô calculus says otherwise for Brownian motion:
$dt\,dW \approx dt^{3/2}$ and $dW\,dW = dt$. Squaring noise is not
infinitesimal at all; it produces a first-order term.

**As equations.** The Itô table has four entries, of which two are non-zero:

<div class="table-wrap">

| | $dW$ | $dt$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $dW$ | $dt$ | $0$ |
| $dt$ | $0$ | $0$ |

</div>

So for a smooth enough $F$, the second-order term in the Itô formula is

$$
\frac{1}{2}\,\partial_i\partial_j F \,\frac{dW_i\,dW_j}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\,\partial_i\partial_j F\,dt,
$$

which is what makes the equation self-consistent: the second derivative term
from the PDE cancels the correction from the product rule.

**As a picture.** Deterministic heat flow spreads a bump smoothly and
predictably. The same equation with multiplicative noise has a random
amplitude at every point, and because the product rule leaks, the evolution
remembers every fluctuation it has ever experienced. That memory is the whole
subject.

**Worked example (U).** Solve $\mathrm{d}X_t = \sigma X_t\,\mathrm{d}W_t$ by
the Itô formula on $F(x) = \log x$:

$$
\mathrm{d}\log X_t = \frac{1}{X_t}\sigma X_t\,\mathrm{d}W_t
 - \frac{1}{2X_t^2}\sigma^2 X_t^2\,\mathrm{d}t
 = \sigma\,\mathrm{d}W_t - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

so $X_t = X_0 \exp(\sigma W_t - \sigma^2 t/2)$. The drift term $-\sigma^2/2$
is entirely an artefact of the product rule. Removing it would give
$\mathbb{E}[X_t] = X_0 \exp(\sigma^2 t / 2)$; exponential growth; which is
the wrong answer and a standard trap.

## What the deterministic theory actually fails at

The standard deterministic heat equation has a smooth solution for smooth
initial data, and this is proved by energy estimates:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\lVert u \rVert^2_{L^2}
= -\tfrac12 \lVert \partial_x u \rVert^2_{L^2}.
$$

Run the same computation on the stochastic equation and the drift term becomes
$2\xi u \partial_t u$, whose size is bounded by $\lVert \xi\rVert_\infty \lVert u\rVert^2$. **That is the exact point of failure**: white noise is a
distribution, not a function, so $\lVert\xi\rVert_\infty$ does not exist. Saying
it fails "because Gaussian variables exceed every threshold infinitely often"
would be wrong; a Gaussian-valued *function* has perfectly finite $L^p$ norms.
The reason is regularity: $\xi$ has parabolic Hölder regularity
$-\tfrac{3}{2} - \epsilon$ in $1+1$ dimensions, so it is not a function at all and
no pointwise norm of it is defined.

So the failure is structural, not a matter of tighter estimates. Anything
built on $\sup|\xi|$; smoothing, boundary regularity, the standard parabolic
smoothing story; is unavailable, and a different class of methods is needed.

## Three ways in, and why two of them stop

**Kolmogorov's method (A).** Estimate moment bounds

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t \le T} \lVert u(t) \rVert^2_{L^p}\right] \le C
\quad\text{when}\quad \frac{2}{p} + \frac{1}{2} < 1,
$$

that is $p > 4$. This produces a continuous $L^p$-valued solution and is the
classical approach. It works, but it stops exactly where it should: the
solution is a *random element of a coarse Banach space*, not a function. The
noise is integrated, not resolved.

**The Martingale method (A).** Solve the backward problem with an $L^1$ kernel,
bound the maximal inequality, and sum. Yields solutions in $L^\Omega$ spaces
that can be far rougher than $L^p$. Better suited to low regularity, and it is
what makes KPZ-type solutions exist at all.

**Neither gives what physics asks for.** Physicists want pointwise behaviour:
what does the solution do at a *fixed* point as a function of time? Both
methods hand back a random element of a space that says nothing about
pointwise values. Closing that gap needs the subject's central invention.

## Regularity structures and paracontrolled calculus

**The idea (A/R).** Do not try to solve the equation directly. Instead, solve
it *formally* to infinite order, integrating both the nonlinearity and the
noise by whatever Itô calculus offers, and use the cancellations that emerge to
prove that the resulting formal series actually converges. The infinite series
is the solution; convergence is the theorem.

The three ideas that make it work:

- **Local subcriticality.** Noise of regularity $\alpha$ and nonlinearity of
  homogeneity $\beta$ combine into $k\alpha + \beta$. Requiring this $< \beta$
  at every order is the subcriticality condition; it is what makes the
  renormalisation constants finite and the series convergent.
- **Renormalisation.** Where subcriticality fails, a counterterm must be
  subtracted; and in the subcritical case these counterterms are universal,
  depending only on the noise law.
- **Paracontrolled calculus (A/R).** The parallel method: model the solution
  as a sum of objects each controlled with respect to a different part of the
  problem (linear part, noise, resonant part), so that products of unknowns
  become products of *knowns* after subtracting the resonant terms.

**Why this is hard to teach and worth learning.** Every step above is a choice
about which object to regard as "known", and each choice is a bookkeeping
decision that has to be redone from scratch for a new equation. The theory is
less a set of theorems than a way of organising the bookkeeping; which is why
it took until 2011 to formalise, and why it now underpins so much of the field.

## Proofs

One computation, and it is the one the whole page is about: the pointwise variance
of the stochastic convolution, which is finite in one spatial dimension and
infinite in two. The dimension where it diverges is exactly the dimension where
renormalisation becomes necessary, so this single integral locates the critical
dimension and proves that it is critical.

**Theorem.** Let $Z$ solve $\partial_t Z = \partial_x^2 Z + \xi$ with $Z(0) = 0$,
where $\xi$ is space-time white noise. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[Z(t,x)^2\big] =
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{t / 2\pi} & d = 1, \\[4pt]
+\infty & d = 2.
\end{cases}
$$

*Proof.* The solution is the stochastic convolution with the heat kernel,
$Z(t,x) = \int_0^t\!\!\int G(s, y)\,\xi(\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}y)$, and by the
Itô isometry in space-time form,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[Z(t,x)^2\big] = \int_0^t\!\!\int G(s,y)^2\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}s.
$$

Everything from here is the heat kernel. In $d$ dimensions
$G(s,y) = (4\pi s)^{-d/2}\,e^{-|y|^2/4s}$, so

$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} G(s,y)^2\,\mathrm{d}y
= \frac{1}{(4\pi s)^{d}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-|y|^2/2s}\,\mathrm{d}y
= \frac{(2\pi s)^{d/2}}{(4\pi s)^{d}}
= \frac{1}{(8\pi s)^{d/2}}.
$$

The remaining integral over $s$ is
$\int_0^t (8\pi s)^{-d/2}\,\mathrm{d}s$, which converges at the origin iff
$d/2 < 1$, i.e. iff $d = 1$. So:

$$
d = 1:\quad \int_0^t \frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\sqrt{8\pi s}}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi}} \cdot 2\sqrt{t} = \sqrt{\frac{t}{2\pi}},
\qquad
d = 2:\quad \int_0^t \frac{\mathrm{d}s}{8\pi s} = +\infty.
$$

$\blacksquare$

The logarithmic divergence in $d = 2$ is not a pathology of a bad estimate; the
integral genuinely diverges, so $Z(t,x)$ is not a random variable with finite
second moment in two dimensions; it is a distribution, of negative Hölder
regularity, and no pointwise product with itself is defined.

**What this buys the page's central claim.** For $\Phi^4_2$,
$\partial_t u = \partial_x^2 u - u^3 + \xi$, write $u = Z + v$ with $Z$ the linear
solution above. Then

$$
u^3 = v^3 + 3v^2 Z + 3 v Z^2 + Z^3,
$$

and the terms $Z^2$ and $Z^3$ involve the pointwise square and cube of an object
that is not a function; which is what the integral above forbids. The
renormalised equation subtracts $3 C_\delta\, u_\delta$ where
$C_\delta = \mathbb{E}[Z_\delta^2] \to \infty$ is the smeared-out version of the
divergent integral: mollify $\xi$ at scale $\delta$ and $C_\delta$ is finite but
grows without bound as $\delta \to 0$. In $d=1$ the same computation gives
$C_\delta$ converging, which is why $\Phi^4_1$ needed no renormalisation and why
the stochastic heat equation is a genuine function there.

So the theorem above is the reason the section on renormalisation exists: the
critical dimension is exactly where this integral stops converging, and that is
read off from the exponent of $s$ rather than from any deep regularity theory.
The general statement; that subcriticality is a condition on regularities
$\alpha, \beta$ combining as $k\alpha + \beta$; is the same computation carried
out term by term for every product appearing in the nonlinearity, with the heat
kernel scaling doing all the work.

## Counterexamples

<div class="table-wrap">

| Claim | True? | Counterexample |
| ----- | ----- | -------------- |
| The deterministic heat equation has a smooth solution for smooth data | no, once noise is multiplicative | white noise is in no $L^p$, so every estimate on $\sup\lVert\xi\rVert$ is void |
| Stochastic PDE solutions are smooth in time | no | the stochastic heat equation's solution is Hölder continuous in time with exponent $< \tfrac{1}{4}$, and that exponent is sharp |
| The Wick product solves all the renormalisation problems | no | it is canonical in the subcritical Ginzburg–Landau case; for KPZ-type equations the correct renormalisation is not the Wick product, and getting it wrong changes the answer |
| Stochastic integration is the same as ordinary integration in the limit of small steps | no | Itô's correction is $-\sigma^2 t/2$; dropping it gives exponential growth instead of geometric Brownian motion |
| Solutions of SPDEs are functions pointwise | not from the classical methods | Kolmogorov and Martingale methods give random elements of coarse spaces; pointwise behaviour needs regularity structures |
| More smoothing happens with more noise | no | noise destroys smoothing, it does not add it |
| Uniqueness holds automatically | no | uniqueness is a theorem requiring subcriticality, and it fails outside it |

</div>

The second row is the sharpest statement in the table: the Hölder exponent
$<\tfrac{1}{4}$ in time is not a weakness of a proof but the true regularity
of the solution, and reaching it was a genuine discovery rather than a
technical estimate.

## Where the research frontier is

- **The KPZ equation** and the directed landscape. The KPZ equation is the
  universal scaling limit of interacting particle systems, and it sits exactly
  in the supercritical regime where the Wick product is the wrong
  renormalisation. Recent work identifies the whole landscape of solutions,
  not just the fixed-point one, and connects it to the Yang–Lee Hamiltonian.
- **Three-dimensional quantum Yang–Mills via stochastic quantisation.** The
  programme is to construct a four-dimensional superfield gauge theory as a
  stochastic PDE on the three-dimensional Minkowski space and prove the
  continuum limit exists. Rigorous partial results exist; the full continuum
  limit is open.
- **Dynamic $\Phi^4_3$**, where the construction is complete but the
  universality classes and critical exponents are still being established.
- **Renormalisation group as a semi-group.** The question of when
  renormalisation converges and what the limit depends on is open in general,
  not merely in specific models.
- **Freedman's inequality and stochastic integrability**, where the best
  current bounds lose powers of the distance to criticality that sharp
  results would want.

## Interleaving problems

Mix these with [Itô
Integration](/14-graduate-stochastic-analysis/1_ito-integration-and-formula/),
[Measure Theory](/10-measure-theory/2_measures/),
[Functional Analysis](/11-functional-analysis/1_normed-spaces-and-banach-spaces/),
[Ricci Flow](/16-graduate-geometry/1_ricci-flow-and-geometrisation/) and
[Limit Theorems](/8-probability-and-statistics/4_limit-theorems/).

1. (Itô.) Solve $\mathrm{d}X_t = X_t^2\,\mathrm{d}W_t$ by taking logarithms
   where you can, and explain exactly where and why the Itô correction
   appears. Compare with the same ODE under ordinary calculus.
2. (Measure theory.) Show that space-time white noise on $[0,T]\times[0,1]$
   is not an element of $L^p$ for any $p$, by computing the distribution of
   its values on a small interval. This is the calculation that kills the
   deterministic proof.
3. (Functional analysis.) State and prove the Banach-valued Itô isometry, and
   use it to show that $\int_0^T \xi_s\,ds$ is Gaussian. Then explain why the
   deterministic energy estimate needs an $L^\infty$ norm that the previous
   problem showed does not exist.
4. (Limit theorems.) Show that $\sup_{t\le T}\lVert u(t)\rVert_{L^p}$ is
   finite for $p>4$ in the multiplicative case, and identify the exponent in
   the Kolmogorov condition as coming from where.
5. (Ricci flow.) Percolation on a graph and Ricci flow are related through the
   same renormalisation-group structure. Describe the analogy and say what
   makes it more than a coincidence; and where it fails.
6. (Research.) Take the SPDE $\partial_t u = \partial_x^2 u + u^3$ and decide
   whether it is subcritical in the sense above. Then explain what goes wrong
   when it is not, and identify the renormalisation counterterm that regularises
   it.

## Peter Weyl Theorem
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/15-graduate-representation-theory/2_peter-weyl-theorem/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "mathematics", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "15 Graduate Representation Theory", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/15-graduate-representation-theory"}, {"name": "2_peter-weyl-theorem", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/15-graduate-representation-theory/2_peter-weyl-theorem"}]
}
</script>

The Peter–Weyl theorem is what finite-group representation theory becomes when
the group is allowed to be infinite; provided it is compact. For a finite group
there are finitely many irreducible representations, they are indexed by
conjugacy classes, and their characters are orthonormal in an averaging inner
product. For a compact group there are still finitely many in each dimension,
they are still orthogonal, and the averaging inner product becomes an integral
against Haar measure. Everything finite-group theory established survives, with
sums replaced by integrals; and the theorem adds something the finite case
cannot see: completeness, which is the statement that there is nothing else.

The reason to prove it rather than cite it is that the proof is a
translation exercise. It is the finite-group theory of
[the previous page](/15-graduate-representation-theory/1_representation-theory-of-finite-groups/)
with `sum over g` replaced by `integral over G`; and the two steps where the
infinite case genuinely differs are the two steps worth understanding: where
density is needed in place of finiteness, and where a *finite* subgroup
approximation makes the result concrete.

## Intuition

Take the circle group $S^1$. Its irreducible representations are the characters
$\chi_n(z) = z^n$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and the Peter–Weyl theorem says these
are an orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^1)$; which is exactly Fourier theory, read
as representation theory. The theorem is the statement that Fourier analysis is
the representation theory of $S^1$, and that this is not a coincidence: every
compact group has a "Fourier theory", its irreducible representations, and the
expansion of a function in that basis is its Fourier series.

Now take $SU(2)$. Its irreducibles are indexed by a non-negative integer $n$, of
dimension $n+1$, and Peter–Weyl says their matrix coefficients are an
orthonormal basis of $L^2(SU(2))$; so a function on the group decomposes into
components of definite "spin", which is why angular momentum in quantum
mechanics is the representation theory of $SU(2)$ read backwards. That is the
sentence this page exists to make precise.

The completeness is what makes the analogy arithmetic. Orthonormality alone
says the irreducibles are a nicely separated family; completeness says they are
*all* of them, so counting representations counts everything and, applied to the
regular representation, forces $\sum_i d_i^2 = 1$-type identities to hold with
integrals in place of sums.

## 1. Haar measure, and what compactness buys

**Definition.** A **Haar measure** $\mu$ on a compact group $G$ is a regular
Borel measure, invariant under left translation, with $\mu(G) = 1$. It exists
and is unique.

Compactness is the load-bearing hypothesis in three places, and it is worth
listing them before using them:

1. $\mu(G) = 1$; the total mass is finite, so $L^2(G, \mu)$ is a Hilbert space
   with the inner product $\langle f_1, f_2\rangle = \int f_1 \overline{f_2}\,d\mu$,
   the direct analogue of averaging over a finite group.
2. Every irreducible representation is finite-dimensional. This is *false* for
   non-compact groups; the regular representation of $\mathbb{R}$ decomposes
   into characters of continuous cardinality, none of them square-integrable -
   and it is the reason the theorem is stated for compact groups only.
3. Compact groups have plenty of finite group quotients, which is what makes
   the approximation argument in Section 4 work.

**Unimodularity.** For compact $G$, left Haar measure is also right-invariant:
$\mu(Eg) = \mu(E)$. The reason is that right translation by a fixed element is an
automorphism, so $\nu(E) = \mu(Eg)$ is another left-Haar measure, and by
uniqueness $\nu = c\mu$ for a constant $c$; iterating gives $c^n = 1$ unless
$c = 1$, and since $\mu$ is finite and $c > 0$, compactness forces $c = 1$.
Unimodularity is what lets $\rho(g)^{-1} = \rho(g^{-1}) = \overline{\rho(g)}{}^{\,t}$
pass through integrals without a modular function appearing.

## 2. Schur's lemma, and unitarity

**Lemma 1 (unitarisation).** Every finite-dimensional representation of a
compact group is unitarisable: there is an inner product on $V$ with
$\rho(g)$ unitary for all $g$.

*Proof.* Take any inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_0$ on $V$ and average
it over the group:

$$
\langle v, w\rangle = \int_G \langle \rho(h)v, \rho(h)w\rangle_0\,d\mu(h).
$$

This is an inner product, and invariance of $\mu$ gives

$$
\langle \rho(g)v, \rho(g)w\rangle
= \int_G \langle \rho(hg)v, \rho(hg)w\rangle_0\,d\mu(h)
= \int_G \langle \rho(k)v, \rho(k)w\rangle_0\,d\mu(k) = \langle v, w\rangle
$$

after the change of variable $k = hg$. $\blacksquare$

The averaging trick is exactly the one from the finite case, with the sum
replaced by an integral; and this is the first place compactness is used, since
the integral converges only because $\mu(G) = 1$.

**Lemma 2 (Schur).** If $V, W$ are irreducible unitary representations and
$\varphi : V \to W$ is $G$-linear, then $\varphi = 0$ unless $V \cong W$, in
which case $\varphi = \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$.

*Proof.* Identical to the finite case: $\ker\varphi$ and
$\operatorname{im}\varphi$ are closed $G$-invariant subspaces, so irreducibility
makes each trivial or everything. For the self-map case, unitarity lets
$\varphi$ be replaced by a self-adjoint or skew one without losing
$G$-linearity; a self-adjoint operator has a spectral projection, which is
$G$-invariant and neither $0$ nor $I$ unless $\varphi$ is scalar. $\blacksquare$

Notice what changed and what did not. The finite-dimensional conclusion survives
because of compactness, not because the group is finite; and the spectral
projection replaces the eigenvalue argument, since a $G$-linear operator on an
infinite-dimensional space need have no eigenvalues at all.

## 3. Orthogonality of matrix coefficients

For irreducible unitary $\rho : G \to U(V)$ of dimension $d_\rho$, choose an
orthonormal basis and write the matrix coefficients
$\rho_{ij}(g) = \langle \rho(g)e_j, e_i\rangle$. These are functions in
$L^2(G, \mu)$, and:

**Theorem (orthogonality).**

$$
\int_G \rho_{ij}(g)\,\overline{\rho'_{kl}(g)}\,d\mu(g)
= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}}{d_\rho} & \rho \cong \rho' \\[6pt] 0 & \rho \not\cong \rho'. \end{cases}
$$

*Proof.* Fix $w \in W$ and consider $T : V \to W$, $T(v) = \langle v, w\rangle v_0$
for a fixed $v_0 \in W$. Average it:

$$
\varphi = \int_G \rho'(h)\,T\,\rho(h)^{-1}\,d\mu(h).
$$

Then $\varphi$ is $G$-linear: for $g \in G$,
$\rho'(g)\varphi\rho(g)^{-1} = \int \rho'(hg)T\rho(hg)^{-1}d\mu(h) = \varphi$
by left invariance. By Schur, $\varphi = 0$ if $V \not\cong W$ and
$\varphi = \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ if $V = W$.

Taking $V = W$ and taking traces computes $\lambda$:
$\operatorname{tr}\varphi = \lambda d_\rho$, while
$\operatorname{tr}T = \langle v_0, w\rangle$ is preserved by conjugation, so
$\operatorname{tr}\varphi = \operatorname{tr}T$. Hence
$\lambda = \langle v_0, w\rangle/d_\rho$, and reading off the $(i,j)$ entry of
$\varphi$ with $v_0 = e_i$, $w = e_j$ gives the second line. For
$V \not\cong W$, $\varphi = 0$ gives the vanishing directly. $\blacksquare$

## 4. Completeness: the Peter–Weyl theorem

**Theorem (Peter–Weyl, 1927).** The union of the spaces of matrix coefficients
of all irreducible unitary representations is dense in $L^2(G, \mu)$.
Consequently these spaces are pairwise orthogonal and their direct sum is
everything:

$$
L^2(G, \mu) = \widehat{\bigoplus}_{\rho \in \widehat{G}} \; \mathrm{End}(V_\rho),
\qquad
\dim \mathrm{End}(V_\rho) = d_\rho^2.
$$

*Proof (dense, then closed under the wrong assumption).* Suppose the span $\mathcal{C}$
of all matrix coefficients is not dense. Then some $f \in L^2(G)$, $f \neq 0$, is
orthogonal to $\mathcal{C}$, and since $\mathcal{C}$ is an algebra of continuous
functions that separates points and contains constants, the two-variable Stone–
Weierstrass theorem makes $\mathcal{C}$ dense in $C(G \times G)$ on
$\{(x,y) : x = y\}$, hence; by applying it to $f$'s_translate; dense in
$C(G)$ in the uniform norm.

Since $L^2$ convergence implies convergence in measure, $f$ orthogonal to a
uniformly dense subset of $C(G)$ forces $f = 0$ almost everywhere: for any
continuous $h$ there is $c_n \in \mathcal{C}$ with $c_n \to h$ uniformly, so
$\int f\overline{h} = \lim_n \int f \overline{c_n} = 0$, and continuous functions
are dense in $L^2$, so $f = 0$. Contradiction.

For the separation step: given distinct $x, y \in G$, an irreducible
representation with $\rho(x) \neq \rho(y)$ must exist, or else all matrix
coefficients agree on $x$ and $y$ and nothing in $\mathcal{C}$ separates them.
That irreducible representations separate points is the Gelfand–Raikov theorem,
proved in outline in
**[Banach Algebras and the Gelfand Representation](/12-graduate-analysis/2_banach-algebras-and-the-gelfand-representation/)**:
a continuous positive-definite function built from a neighbourhood of the
identity avoiding $g$, read as a matrix coefficient of the cyclic representation
its translates generate. What this page uses is the consequence: $\mathcal{C}$
separates points and Stone–Weierstrass applies. This is also the only step
where compactness is essential rather than convenient, and it is why the theorem
fails for $\mathbb{R}$: an infinite-dimensional irreducible representation of
$\mathbb{R}$ exists, and the conclusion is false there. $\blacksquare$

## 5. What the finite case sees, and what it cannot

Setting $G$ finite recovers the finite-group results exactly: Haar measure is
counting measure divided by $|G|$, so the integrals are averages, and
$\dim\mathrm{End}(V_\rho) = d_\rho^2$ summed over irreducibles gives
$|G| = \sum_i d_i^2$ again.

What the finite case cannot see is the *completeness*. For a finite group,
finiteness of the number of irreducibles is automatic from
$|G| = \sum d_i^2$; for a compact group it is a theorem, and it has content:
the irreducibles of $S^1$ are indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$, infinitely many but
discretely, which is why Fourier series work. For $\mathbb{R}$ the index set
becomes $\mathbb{R}$ itself and the sum becomes an integral; the Fourier
*transform*; and that is exactly where the theorem stops applying, since those
characters are not in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

**Consequence: characters are complete.** Since characters are sums of diagonal
matrix coefficients, and matrix coefficients are dense, two irreducible
representations with the same character are isomorphic, and a representation is
determined by its character. For a finite group that followed from finiteness;
here it is the Peter–Weyl theorem speaking.

**Consequence: every compact group is an inverse limit of images in unitary
groups.** The separating family of representations embeds $G$ into a product of
unitary groups, and the finite-dimensional quotients give
$G \cong \varprojlim G/N$ over the normal subgroups $N$ with $G/N$ a Lie group.
Compact groups are, in this precise sense, approximable by finite groups; which
is why finite-group intuition transfers, and why it transfers *only* through
limit arguments rather than by direct analogy.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Assuming irreducibles are finite-dimensional for non-compact groups.** They
  are not, and the theorem is false there: $\mathbb{R}$ has no
  finite-dimensional non-trivial unitary representations at all, since
  $\mathbb{R}$ is abelian and its unitary characters $e^{i\xi x}$ are
  non-integrable.
- **Reading $\widehat\oplus$ as an ordinary sum.** The direct sum is
  *Hilbert-space* completion of the algebraic direct sum: an
  $L^2$ function is a square-summable *sequence of coefficients*, not a finite
  combination. Fourier series converge in $L^2$, not pointwise in general.
- **Using eigenvalues where spectral projections are needed.** On an
  infinite-dimensional irreducible, a $G$-linear operator need have no
  eigenvalues; Schur's lemma is proved with a spectral projection, and the
  finite-group proof does not transfer verbatim.
- **Treating $\mu(G) = 1$ as a convention.** It is what makes $L^2(G)$ a
  Hilbert space containing the constants, and what makes the orthogonality
  relations normalised the same way as the finite case. Changing it changes
  every formula.
- **Forgetting unimodularity.** For a non-unimodular group the left and right
  regular representations differ by the modular function, and the orthogonality
  relations pick up a Jacobian. Compact groups are unimodular, which is why the
  relations above are clean.
- **Expecting pointwise convergence of the expansion.** Peter–Weyl gives $L^2$
  convergence. Pointwise convergence of the Fourier expansion of a continuous
  function on $S^1$ *fails* in general, and the same is true on every compact
  group.

## Applications

- **Harmonic analysis on compact groups.** Every compact group has a Fourier
  theory; the irreducibles index the "frequencies", and convolution becomes
  pointwise multiplication of matrix coefficients after the transform.
- **Angular momentum.** The irreducibles of $SU(2)$ are indexed by
  $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ with dimension $n + 1$, matching the spin degeneracies of
  quantum mechanics; Peter–Weyl is why a wavefunction on $SU(2)$ decomposes into
  components of definite spin.
- **Number theory.** Automorphic forms are functions on quotient spaces
  $\Gamma \backslash G$ for compact $G$; their spectral expansion is
  Peter–Weyl applied to the right regular representation, and the Langlands
  program is in large part the study of what replaces it in the non-compact case.
- **Random walks on groups.** Convergence of a random walk to the uniform
  distribution is a statement about powers of the projection onto the
  non-trivial isotypic components, which Peter–Weyl supplies; the upper bound
  lemma of Diaconis–Shahshahani is character orthogonality applied to this.
- **Compact quantum groups.** Woronowicz's theory is Peter–Weyl with the algebra
  of functions replaced by a non-commutative one, and the theorem's statement
  survives almost unchanged.

## Cross-References

- **[Homomorphisms and Isomorphism Theorems](/1-abstract-algebra/5_homomorphisms-and-isomorphism-theorems/)**; quotients, which is what the inverse-limit statement is made of.
- **[Normed Spaces and Banach Spaces](/11-functional-analysis/1_normed-spaces-and-banach-spaces/)**; completeness of $L^2$, which is what the Hilbert direct sum needs.
- **[Compactness](/9-topology/5_compactness/)**; the hypothesis doing the work in all three places it is used.
- **[The Fundamental Theorems](/11-functional-analysis/4_the-fundamental-theorems/)**; the spectral theorem, of which Peter–Weyl is the group-representation specialisation.
- [Quantum Mechanics](https://physics.wyattau.com/5-quantum-mechanics/); spin, which is the representation theory of $SU(2)$ read backwards.
- [Fourier Series](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/7_fourier-series/); the $S^1$ case, met first without the representation-theoretic language.
