**The Defect.** Stage C proved that no rational measures the diagonal of
the unit square, while density says the rationals have no gaps between
their elements. Both are true, and together they are intolerable: the
diagonal is a length, lengths form a line, and a line with no gaps
between its points should contain every length on it. The naive
conjecture is that this is a technicality: "just add the missing
lengths". But what *is* a missing length? A symbol? An infinite decimal?
A limit of approximations? None of those can be the definition, because
each presupposes the line it is meant to create. The repair is Dedekind's
move, and it is characteristically backwards: a real number is *nothing
but* a cut in the rationals, a clean dividing of all rationals into left
and right. The line is not repaired. It is rebuilt, from the order alone,
and completeness comes out as a theorem instead of a hope.

**The One-Line Reveal.** <span class="wn-spoiler-inline" tabindex="0">A
real number is a perfect way of splitting the rationals into below and
above; the set of all such splits is ordered, complete by construction,
contains every rational, measures every length including the diagonal,
and the same cut-and-climb machinery that builds it (ordinals,
transfinite induction, choice) becomes the toolkit for everything
after.</span>

*The blur is deliberate: form your own reading of the page first, then
click it.*

**Scope.** Consumes Stage C (the rationals, their order and density, the
crisis) and Stage B (arithmetic, well-ordering, the recursion principle).
One declaration is adopted: the **axiom of choice** (Section 6), recorded
in the course map's axiom table alongside classical logic, and never
silently assumed. No debts are declared on this page; one is *paid*:
Stage B's recursion-principle debt, whose general form is Stage D's
transfinite recursion (Section 5), is discharged here in the course map's
ledger. Formal witnesses pause for this stage: the constructions live
past core Lean's built-ins, and resume when the course returns to
decidable ground.

## 1. Dedekind Cuts: the Line from Order Alone

**The naive conjecture.** A real number is an infinite decimal, or a
limit of rationals, or "whatever the diagonal measures". Each candidate
presupposes a notion of convergence or distance that belongs to the very
line being built. The repair uses only what already exists: the rationals
and their order. A length is fully described by which rationals fall
below it, so *be* that description.

**Definition (cut).** A **cut** is a set $\alpha \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$
such that: $\alpha \neq \varnothing$ and $\alpha \neq \mathbb{Q}$
(nonempty, proper); if $q \in \alpha$ and $p < q$ then $p \in \alpha$
(closed downward); and $\alpha$ has **no greatest element** (for every
$q \in \alpha$ some $r \in \alpha$ has $q < r$). The set of all cuts is
called $\mathbb{R}$.

**Definition (the embedding).** Each rational $q$ becomes the cut $q^* :=
\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r < q\}$. Every property of cuts holds for $q^*$
by density of $\mathbb{Q}$ (Stage C: between any two rationals another),
so $\mathbb{Q}$ sits inside $\mathbb{R}$ without changing its arithmetic.

**Definition (order).** $\alpha \leq \beta$ means $\alpha \subseteq
\beta$ (as sets). This is an order: reflexive, antisymmetric (mutual
containment is set equality), transitive by chaining inclusions.

**Theorem (the order extends the rationals').** For rationals $p, q$:
$p < q$ if and only if $p^* \subsetneq q^*$.

*Proof.* If $p < q$, then $p \in q^*$ but $p \notin p^*$ (a cut has no
greatest element, so its own boundary point $p$ is excluded), giving
proper containment. Conversely, if $p^* \subsetneq q^*$, pick $r \in
q^*$ outside $p^*$; then $r < q$ and $r \geq p$, so $p \leq r < q$ gives
$p < q$. $\blacksquare$

**Ponder.** Before reading on: the definition insists a cut has no
greatest element. Why? Try defining cuts *with* greatest elements
allowed, and consider the set $\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r \leq 1\}$ versus
$\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r < 1\}$. Both should represent "one". What goes
wrong?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>The autopsy</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

With greatest elements allowed, the number $1$ would be cut twice: once
as the set ending at (and including) $1$, once as the set ending just
before it. Two distinct objects representing one number breaks
extensionality, the bedrock of Stage A. Excluding the greatest element
is the choice that makes each cut a *unique* description: the boundary
itself always lives on the right side, and the rationals embed exactly.
The alternative repair, quotienting by "cuts with the same boundary",
would work but adds a quotient stage for no benefit.

</div>
</details>

:::note[Quick check]

1. State the three conditions defining a cut.
2. Why does density of $\mathbb{Q}$ make the embedding $q \mapsto q^*$
   honest?
3. In the order on cuts, what does $\alpha \leq \beta$ mean set-wise?
4. Why is $p \notin p^*$ for any rational $p$?
5. Which Stage C theorem does the cut construction *not* need, and why
   is that important?
6. Verify that $\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r < 1\}$ is a cut by checking all
   four conditions (where does density earn its keep?).
7. Write out $0^*$ and $1^*$ as sets, and decide $0^* < 1^*$ by
   containment.
8. Which rational is the boundary of $q^*$, and which side of the cut
   is it on?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">
1. Nonempty, proper, closed downward, no greatest element.
2. It ensures every cut boundary is approachable from inside by rationals, so rationals and their cuts behave identically in the order.
3. $\alpha \subseteq \beta$.
4. A cut contains only rationals strictly below its boundary, and $p$ is the boundary of $p^*$.
5. The crisis theorem is not needed: the cut construction does not presuppose that holes exist, only builds the line that will measure them.
6. Nonempty ($0$ is in); proper ($2$ is out); downward closed (anything below a member is still below $1$); no greatest element, and here density does the work: any member $r < 1$ has a larger rational still below $1$.
7. $0^* = \{r : r < 0\}$ and $1^* = \{r : r < 1\}$; $0^* \subsetneq 1^*$ (the rational $0$ belongs to the second but not the first), so $0^* < 1^*$.
8. The boundary is $q$ itself, and it lives on the right: outside the cut, which is exactly the no-greatest-element condition.
</div>
</details>

:::

## 2. Arithmetic and Completeness: the Summit

**Ponder 1 (invent addition on cuts).** Before reading the definition:
a cut is a set of rationals, so arithmetic on cuts must be built from
arithmetic on rationals. Invent addition: given two cuts $\alpha$ and
$\beta$, which set of rationals should deserve the name $\alpha +
\beta$? Test your candidate against the requirement that $q^* + r^*$
should equal $(q + r)^*$.

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Compare your construction</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

The natural candidate: add elementwise. $\alpha + \beta$ should be the
set of all sums $r + s$ with $r$ from $\alpha$ and $s$ from $\beta$.
Check it on embedded rationals: the sums of all $r < q$ and all $s < r'
$ are exactly the numbers below $q + r'$ (density closes the gap on
both sides), so $q^* + r'^* = (q + r')^*$: the embedding respects
addition. The work is then proving the elementwise set is a cut and
satisfies the laws, which is what the theorems below do.

</div>
</details>

**Definition (addition).** $\alpha + \beta := \{r + s : r \in \alpha,\
s \in \beta\}$.

**Theorem.** $\alpha + \beta$ is a cut; addition is commutative and
associative; $\alpha + 0^* = \alpha$; and $\alpha + (-\alpha) =
0^*$, where $-\alpha := \{r \in \mathbb{Q} : \text{some } s \notin
\alpha \text{ has } r < -s\}$.

*Proof.* Cut-hood: nonempty (both cuts are), proper (each element is a
sum with $r < $ (boundary of $\alpha$) and $s < $ (boundary of
$\beta$), so every element is below a rational bound outside), closed
downward (smaller sums come from smaller summands), no greatest element
(increase $s$ by density, keeping $r$ fixed). Commutativity is
commutativity of rational addition; associativity likewise. Identity:
$\alpha + 0^* = \{r + 0 : r \in \alpha\} = \alpha$ since every element
of a cut can be increased within it. Inverse: the negative cut is a
genuine cut, and $r + s = 0$ with $r \in \alpha$, $s \notin \alpha$
defines exactly the pairing $0^*$ requires; the no-greatest-element
condition on both sides closes the boundary. The full element-chase for
the inverse is Problem 1. $\blacksquare$

**Definition (multiplication).** For positive cuts $\alpha, \beta$
(those containing some $q > 0$): $\alpha \times \beta := \{r \times s :
r \in \alpha, s \in \beta, r > 0, s > 0\} \cup \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q
\leq 0\}$. Multiplication of arbitrary cuts is then defined by the
sign cases, using $-\alpha$ from Section 2, exactly as sign cases work
for integers.

**Theorem.** Multiplication of positive cuts is a cut; it is
commutative, associative, distributes over addition; $1^*$ is the
multiplicative identity; and every positive cut has a multiplicative
inverse.

*Proof.* Cut-hood and the laws mirror the addition proof with rational
multiplication in place of addition; each rational law used is Stage C's
(Theorem, inherited from Stage B). The inverse of a positive $\alpha$
is $-\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : \text{some } s \in \alpha \text{ has } q <
1/s\}$ (the reciprocals of the *non*-members, negated); verifying
$\alpha \times \alpha^{-1} = 1^*$ is a two-sided density chase and is
Problem 2. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (completeness: the summit).** Every nonempty set of cuts,
bounded above, has a **least upper bound** in $\mathbb{R}$.

*Proof.* Let $T$ be a nonempty set of cuts, bounded above by a cut
$\beta$. Define $\sigma := \bigcup T$, the union of all cuts in $T$.
$\sigma$ is a set of rationals; claim it is a cut. Nonempty: $T$ is
nonempty, so $\sigma$ contains a cut's worth. Proper: every element of
$\sigma$ lies in some member of $T$, hence below $\beta$'s boundary, so
$\sigma \subseteq \beta \neq \mathbb{Q}$; and $\sigma$ cannot be all of
$\mathbb{Q}$ or no $\beta$ bounded it. Closed downward: if $r \in
\sigma$ and $p < r$, then $r$ lies in some $\alpha \in T$, and $\alpha$
closed downward puts $p \in \alpha \subseteq \sigma$. No greatest
element: if $r \in \sigma$, pick $\alpha \in T$ with $r \in \alpha$;
$\alpha$ has no greatest element, so some $r' \in \alpha$ has $r <
r'$, and $r' \in \sigma$. So $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$. It is an upper
bound: $\sigma$ contains every member of $T$. It is least: any other
upper bound $\beta'$ contains every member of $T$, hence contains their
union $\sigma$. $\blacksquare$

This is the theorem the whole course has been climbing toward, and it is
three paragraphs. The reason it is so short: Dedekind's definition made
"least upper bound" mean "the union", and unions are easy.

**Theorem (the crisis resolved).** There is a real number $\alpha$
with $\alpha \times \alpha = 2$, that is, the diagonal of the unit
square has a measure.

*Proof.* Define $\alpha := \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q < 0 \text{ or } q
\times q < 2\}$. Then $\alpha$ is a cut (nonempty, proper, downward
closed; no greatest element, because for $q > 0$ in $\alpha$ with $q
\times q < 2$, some larger rational still has square below $2$, by
density and the continuity of squaring on small rational steps.
Explicitly, if $q \times q < 2$ then $q < h$ for a rational $h$ with
$h \times h < 2$, constructed by taking $h$ slightly larger than $q$;
the explicit rational is $(q \times 2 + 2)/(q + 2)$, and checking $h
\times h < 2$ is Stage B algebra). Now compute $\alpha \times \alpha$
with the positive-cut definition: every element below a positive $q$
with $q \times q < 2$ paired with itself gives products below $2$, and
every positive rational $s$ with $s \times s < 2$ lies in $\alpha$;
the cut $\alpha \times \alpha$ is exactly $\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q <
2\}$'s positive part, which is $2^*$. Hence $\alpha \times \alpha =
2^*$: the diagonal measures $\alpha$. $\blacksquare$

The cut $\alpha$ is, of course, what the world calls $\sqrt{2}$. Stage C
proved no rational does this job; the cuts do it without strain, and
that is the entire justification of the construction.

**The tower so far.** One table holds the whole climb; each row is the
construction move this course spent a stage proving:

| System | Built from | Defining rule | New power |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathbb{N}$ (Stage B) | five declarations | the induction licence | counting, induction, well-ordering |
| $\mathbb{Z}$ (Stage C) | pairs of counting numbers | $a + d = c + b$ | subtraction total |
| $\mathbb{Q}$ (Stage C) | pairs of integers, denominator nonzero | $p \times q' = p' \times q$ | division total |
| $\mathbb{R}$ (this stage) | cuts of rationals | downward closed, no greatest element | completeness |

Every embedding in the tower is faithful (the old arithmetic is
unchanged inside the new system), and each stage's hard theorem is the
next stage's raw material.

:::note[Quick check]

1. State the three cut conditions.
2. What is $q^*$, and why does $\mathbb{Q}$ embed?
3. State completeness in one sentence, and identify which object in
   the proof *is* the supremum.
4. Why is the completeness proof so short?
5. Which Stage C theorem does Section 2's last theorem retire?
6. In the $\sqrt{2}$ cut $\alpha$, is the rational $1.4$ a member? Is
   $1.5$?
7. What is the union $\bigcup \{q^* : q \in \mathbb{Q},\ q < 1/2\}$ as
   a set, and which real is it?
8. Why can the completeness proof not fail to produce an *upper* bound?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">
1. Nonempty, proper, downward closed, no greatest element.
2. The cut $\{r : r < q\}$; every rational law holds in its cut, so the embedding is faithful.
3. Every nonempty bounded-above set of cuts has a least upper bound; the supremum is the union of the set.
4. Dedekind's definition made "least upper bound" mean "the union of the cuts", and unions of downward-closed proper sets are themselves cuts.
5. The crisis theorem: the diagonal now has a real measure.
6. $1.4 \times 1.4 = 1.96 < 2$, so $1.4 \in \alpha$; $1.5 \times 1.5 = 2.25 > 2$, so $1.5 \notin \alpha$.
7. The union is $\{r \in \mathbb{Q} : r < 1/2\}$ (every member of a $q^*$ with $q < 1/2$ is itself below $1/2$, and every $r < 1/2$ lies in some $q^*$ by density): the cut $(1/2)^*$, the real we call one half.
8. The union contains every member of the set by construction: $\sigma \supseteq \alpha$ for each $\alpha \in T$ is exactly what union means, so being an upper bound is not an extra fact to verify but the definition read aloud.
</div>
</details>

:::

## 3. Decimals: Every Real Gets a Name

**Ponder 1 (invent the naming scheme).** Before reading the
definition: every real must get a decimal name, but "infinite decimal"
is not yet a defined object. Invent the digits: given the cut $x$,
which rational quantity should the $k$-th digit record? (Hint: you may
use completeness to grab whole units, tenths, hundredths, one tier at a
time.)

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Compare your construction</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

Tier by tier: completeness hands you the greatest integer below $x$
(the units digit is its last digit); subtract it, multiply by $10$, and
completeness again hands you the greatest integer below that (the
first digit); recurse. Formally, the $k$-th digit is the units digit of
$\lfloor 10^k \times x \rfloor$: each tier is a fresh application of
the greatest-integer construction, which is itself completeness applied
to an integer-bounded set. If your scheme matches, the theorem below
is just the claim that the tiers reassemble.

</div>
</details>

**Definition.** For a real $x$ and a counting number $k$, define the
$k$-th digit function by $d_k(x) :=$ the units digit of
$\lfloor 10^k \times x \rfloor \bmod 10$, where $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$
on cuts is defined as the greatest integer below (a cut-versus-cut
application of completeness to the set $\{z \in \mathbb{Z} : z \leq
x\}$, which is bounded above when $x$ is bounded below by an integer,
and greatest elements exist for integer-bounded cuts).

**Theorem (decimal expansion).** Every real $x \geq 0$ satisfies
$x = \lfloor x \rfloor + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} d_k(x) \times 10^{-k}$,
where the infinite sum means the least upper bound of its finite
partial sums (which exist by completeness, applied to the partial sums
as a bounded set: bounded because each digit contributes less than
$10^{-k}$, and $\sum 10^{-k} < 1$ by Stage B's geometric sum).

*Proof.* The finite truncation through $k$ digits equals
$\lfloor 10^k x \rfloor / 10^k$ exactly (the digit definitions
telescope), and the truncations are nondecreasing in $k$ (each added
digit refines, never lowers, the value), each within $10^{-k}$ of $x$.
The partial sums therefore form a bounded increasing sequence of
rationals; by completeness their least upper bound $\ell$ exists, and
$\ell \leq x \leq \ell + 10^{-k}$ for every $k$; since $10^{-k}$
shrinks with no positive floor (Stage B's Archimedean property applied
to the denominators), $\ell = x$. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (repeating means rational).** A decimal expansion is
eventually periodic exactly when the number it names is rational.

*Proof.* One direction: a rational $p/q$ in lowest terms has decimal
digits driven by the remainders of $10^k \times p$ upon division by
$q$; remainders take values in a finite set (Stage B's remainder
theorem bounds them below $q$), so by the pigeonhole principle some
remainder recurs, and from that point the digits repeat with period at
most $q$. Conversely, an eventually periodic expansion is a finite
decimal plus a geometric series with rational ratio (Stage B's geometric
sum identity closes it in one line), hence rational.
$\blacksquare$

**Ponder.** Before reading on: does $0.999\ldots$ equal $1$?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>The autopsy</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

Yes, and the proof is one line of this stage: $0.999\ldots$ names the
least upper bound of the partial sums $0.9, 0.99, 0.999, \ldots$, each
of which is $1 - 10^{-k}$; the least upper bound of those is $1$, since
anything below $1$ leaves a gap that $10^{-k}$ eventually beats
(Archimedean property). The feeling that "$0.999\ldots$ should be just
under $1$" is the instinct that there is a *last* partial sum; there is
none. The sequence has no final member, and its supremum is the limit
of the names, not the last name. This is the first place the
completeness theorem does visible work, and it does it on a famous
dispute.

</div>
</details>

:::note[Quick check]

1. What does the infinite sum in the decimal theorem *mean*, given that
   Stage B only ever added finitely many terms?
2. Why do the partial sums have a least upper bound?
3. Which Stage B theorem proves that a rational's decimal repeats?
4. State the one-line proof that $0.999\ldots = 1$.
5. Why can two different decimals name the same number, and what is the
   only way?
6. Compute the first three partial sums of $0.999\ldots$ and their
   distances from $1$.
7. Does $1/3 = 0.333\ldots$ contradict the repeating-means-rational
   theorem, or illustrate it?
8. Write the terminating decimal that names $1/2$, and its forbidden
   twin.

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">
1. The least upper bound of the finite partial sums, which exists by completeness.
2. They are nondecreasing and bounded above by $\lfloor x \rfloor + 1$.
3. The pigeonhole principle on the division remainders.
4. It is the least upper bound of $1 - 10^{-k}$, which is $1$.
5. Only when one expansion ends in all $9$s and the other is its terminating twin; the diagonal argument of Section 4 must therefore avoid $9$s.
6. $0.9$, $0.99$, $0.999$, at distances $10^{-1}$, $10^{-2}$, $10^{-3}$ from $1$: shrinking with no floor, which is the Archimedean squeeze.
7. It illustrates the theorem: $1/3$ is rational and its expansion repeats with period $1$ (the remainders of $10^k$ upon division by $3$ are all $1$).
8. $0.5000\ldots$; the twin is $0.4999\ldots$, the recurring-$9$ form of the same real, which the canonical-expansion choice excludes.
</div>
</details>

:::

## 4. Cardinality: Counting the Uncountable

**Definition.** Sets $X$ and $Y$ are **equipotent** (written $X \cong
Y$) when a bijection exists between them. $X$ is **countable** when $X
\cong [n]$ for some counting number $n$, or when $X \cong \mathbb{N}$;
**uncountable** when it is not countable.

**Theorem (countable catalogues).** $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, and
$\mathbb{Q}$ are each countable ($\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{N}$ and
$\mathbb{Q} \cong \mathbb{N}$).

*Proof.* $\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{N}$: interleave, mapping the class
of $(a, b)$ to a single counting number by the pairing recipe (the map
$(a, b) \mapsto 2^a \times 3^b$ composed with a fixed bijection
back from the image is an injection, and $\mathbb{Z}$ is infinite, so
Section 4's Schröder-Bernstein theorem below finishes the bijection).
$\mathbb{Q} \cong \mathbb{N}$: in lowest terms with positive
denominator, map the fraction $p/q$ to $2^{p} \times 3^{q}$ times a
sign factor; again an injection into $\mathbb{N}$, with $\mathbb{Q}$
infinite. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (Schröder-Bernstein).** If $X \cong$ (injects into) $Y$ and
$Y$ injects into $X$, then $X \cong Y$.

*Proof.* Given injections $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to X$, call an
element of $X$ *bad* if tracing backwards through $g$ and $f$
alternately eventually fails on the $X$ side or runs forever starting
from $Y$'s side; define the piecewise map $h$ that follows $g^{-1}$ on
bad elements (where defined) and $f$ elsewhere. The chain decomposition
argument shows $h$ is a well-defined bijection: on bad elements $h =
g^{-1}$ lands in $Y$'s unmatched side; on good elements $h = f$ lands
in $Y$'s matched side; and the two images partition $Y$. The case
analysis is Problem 3. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (Cantor: the diagonal).** No function $f: \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is surjective onto the interval $[0, 1]$ of reals.

*Proof.* Suppose $f$ lists reals $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ in $[0, 1]$,
each with a decimal expansion not ending in recurring $9$s (Section 3
shows every real has exactly one such expansion, choosing the
terminating form when both exist). Build $d$ by: the $k$-th digit of
$d$ is $5$ if the $k$-th digit of $x_k$ is not $5$, and $6$ otherwise.
Then $d \in [0, 1]$ (its digits are $5$ or $6$, so $0 < d < 1$), and
$d$ differs from $x_k$ at digit $k$ for every $k$, differing at a
digit other than $9$ and not $0$ guarantees genuinely different
numbers, dodging the dual-expansion trap. So $d$ is a real no $k$
names. $\blacksquare$

*In words:* assume the list is complete, then walk down the diagonal
taking, at each row, a digit that row failed to use. The walk
manufactures a number every row missed, and choosing digits only from
$\{5, 6\}$ guarantees the miss is genuine rather than a naming
accident of the two-expansion phenomenon.

**Theorem.** The interval $[0, 1]$ is uncountable; so is
$\mathbb{R}$.

*Proof.* Cantor's diagonal: no listing covers $[0, 1]$. And
$\mathbb{R} \cong (0, 1)$ (the map $x \mapsto$ the arctangent-style
bijection via cuts is Problem 4), so uncountability transfers.
$\blacksquare$

**Ponder.** Before reading on: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, $[0, 1]$ is
not, yet between any two rationals the rationals are dense and every
rational sits inside $[0, 1]$. Try to say where the extra elements
hide.

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>The autopsy</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

They hide between the rationals: the irrationals are themselves
uncountable, and no listing of the rationals can be thickened to cover
them. The intuitive picture of "dots on a line" hides the difference
between a dense set and a complete one, which is precisely Stage C's
warning repeated with cardinality attached: density is about between,
completeness is about every point. The diagonal argument does not
merely say the listing missed one point; run it on any listing, and it
manufactures a different missed point each time: uncountably many
manufactured points, no listing survives.

</div>
</details>

:::note[Quick check]

1. Define countable and uncountable.
2. Which theorem lets an injection plus an injection become a
   bijection?
3. Why does the diagonal construction choose digits from $\{5, 6\}$?
4. Is the set of irrationals countable? Justify in one sentence.
5. Which is bigger, $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{N}$? Justify with a
   theorem.
6. Describe an interleaving bijection between $\mathbb{N}$ and
   $\mathbb{Z}$ in words.
7. Running the diagonal construction on a list that contains only
   rationals: where does the manufactured number land?
8. Is the set of terminating decimals countable? Justify.

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">
1. Countable: in bijection with some $[n]$ or with $\mathbb{N}$; uncountable: not.
2. Schröder-Bernstein.
3. To dodge the dual-decimal expansion trap: a digit change outside $\{0, 9\}$ forces a genuinely different number.
4. No: if the irrationals in $[0, 1]$ were countable, their union with the countable rationals would count $[0, 1]$, contradicting Cantor.
5. Equal in size: $\mathbb{Q} \cong \mathbb{N}$ by the injection-and-Schröder-Bernstein argument.
6. Send $0$ to $0$; send the odd counting numbers to the positives ($1 \mapsto 1$, $3 \mapsto 2$, and so on); send the even positives to the negatives ($2 \mapsto -1$, $4 \mapsto -2$, and so on). Every integer is hit exactly once.
7. Outside the rationals: the manufactured number's digits are $5$s and $6$s and need not repeat, so the argument exhibits an irrational the rational-only list never mentioned, with no contradiction.
8. Yes: each terminating decimal is a fraction $m/10^k$; the pairs $(m, k)$ of counting numbers inject into $\mathbb{N}$ (Stage B's pairing bookkeeping), so the terminating decimals inject into a countable set and are countable.
</div>
</details>

:::

## 5. Ordinals and Transfinite Induction: Paying Stage B's Debt

**Definition.** A **well-ordered set** is a set with an order in which
every nonempty subset has a least element. Two well-ordered sets have
the same **order type** when a bijection exists that preserves order in
both directions; an **ordinal** is an order type of a well-ordering.
The empty set's type is $0$; a single point's type is $1$; the type of
$\mathbb{N}$ in its natural order is called $\omega$.

**Theorem (transfinite induction).** Let $P$ be a proposition about the
members of a well-ordered set $W$. If: $P$ holds of the least element
of $W$; and for every $w \in W$, the truth of $P$ on *all* smaller
members implies $P(w)$; then $P$ holds throughout $W$.

*Proof.* Suppose $P$ fails somewhere; the set of failures is nonempty
and has a least member $w_0$ (well-ordering). Every member smaller
than $w_0$ satisfies $P$ (any failure would be smaller than the least
failure). The second hypothesis applies verbatim and gives $P(w_0)$,
contradicting minimality. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (transfinite recursion; Stage B's debt discharged).** For
any recipe that defines a value at $w$ from the values at all smaller
members, there exists exactly one function on $W$ whose value at each
$w$ is given by that recipe.

*Proof sketch.* The full proof builds the function's graph as the
union of all partial approximations (sets of pairs closed under the
recipe), proving by transfinite induction that the approximations
agree wherever they overlap, so the union is a single function; the
argument is Stage B's recursion-principle proof generalised past
$\mathbb{N}$'s single chain into arbitrary well-orderings, where the
"step" may have no immediate predecessor (a **limit position**).
$\blacksquare$

**Ponder.** Before reading on: induction on $\mathbb{N}$ always has a
step "from the previous one". In a general well-ordering there may be
positions with no immediate predecessor (think of $\omega$ itself),
which comes after *all* natural numbers but has none directly before
it. Why does transfinite induction not need a "previous one"?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>The autopsy</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

Because the hypothesis is "all smaller members", not "the immediately
previous member". A limit position $w$ has infinitely many smaller
members, and the hypothesis supplies $P$ on *all of them*; that is
exactly enough to conclude $P(w)$, which is what makes the whole set
closed under the implication. The base case is just the least member's
version of the same rule with an empty "smaller" set. Nothing in the
argument ever needed a step to have a predecessor; that was an
accident of $\mathbb{N}$'s simple shape.

</div>
</details>

:::note[Quick check]

1. Define well-ordered set and ordinal.
2. State transfinite induction.
3. What is a limit position, and why is it harmless?
4. Which Stage B debt does this section discharge, and in which two
   words?
5. Why does the proof of transfinite induction mirror the proof of
   well-ordering's use in Section 3?
6. Exhibit a well-ordered set whose order type is not $\omega$.
7. In that set, which position is a limit position, and what are its
   smaller members?
8. Why is $\mathbb{N}$ with its order reversed not well-ordered?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">
1. Well-ordered: every nonempty subset has a least member; ordinal: the order type of a well-ordering.
2. Base at the least member; at each $w$, truth on all smaller members gives truth at $w$; conclude truth everywhere.
3. A position with no immediate predecessor; the "all smaller members" hypothesis covers it without a predecessor.
4. The recursion principle; paid.
5. Both are least-counterexample arguments; the counterexample set is well-ordered so a least failure exists and contradicts the step hypothesis.
6. Take $\mathbb{N}$ in its usual order and append one new point after all of them: every subset still has a least member, but the order type is past $\omega$ (the world calls it $\omega + 1$).
7. The appended point: its smaller members are all the counting numbers, and it has no immediate predecessor, since no counting number is last.
8. The whole set is a nonempty subset of itself with no least element (the reversed order runs $\ldots, 3, 2, 1, 0$ with no end).
</div>
</details>

:::

## 6. Choice, Zorn's Lemma, and the Well-Ordering Principle

**Ponder 1 (attempt a choice function by hand).** Before reading the
axiom: a family of nonempty sets needs one member picked from each.
For pairs of *shoes*, you can do it without any new axiom: pick the
left shoe. For pairs of *socks* (indistinguishable, no left or right),
try to write the rule. What goes wrong, and what must be adopted to fix
it?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>The obstruction</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

The shoe rule works because a defining property exists: "the left one".
The sock family offers no distinguishing property at all: to choose one
sock from each of infinitely many pairs, you would need either a rule
(there is none that works for an arbitrary family) or a new kind of
licence that asserts the choice exists anyway. That licence is the
axiom of choice. The point of the attempt is that the axiom is not
obvious and not harmless: for *finite* families, Stage A's logic
already proves choice by iterating; the axiom's content is entirely in
the infinite case.

</div>
</details>

**The axiom (choice), adopted.** For every family of nonempty sets
there exists a function choosing one member from each set in the
family. This course adopts choice as an axiom: it is recorded in the
course map's axiom table, it is never silently assumed, and every use
of it is flagged. Two of its famous equivalents are proved below.

**Theorem (Zorn's lemma).** Let $S$ be a partially ordered set in
which every chain (a subfamily any two of whose members are
comparable) has an upper bound in $S$. Then $S$ has a maximal element
(an element with nothing strictly above it).

*Proof.* Suppose $S$ has no maximal element. Then every chain $C$ has
strictly larger candidates: the upper bounds of $C$ are not maximal,
so for each chain there exists a member strictly above the whole
chain. Using choice, select one such strict upper bound above each
chain, uniformly. Now build a chain by transfinite recursion: start
anywhere; at successor positions, take the selected strict upper bound
of what is built; at limit positions, the built family is a chain (the
construction preserves comparability at every stage), so take its
selected strict upper bound. This climbs forever, producing as many
distinct members of $S$ as there are ordinals up to any fixed
well-ordering's type. But $S$ is a set: choosing a well-ordering of a
set large enough to outrun $S$ (which exists, by the same transfinite
machinery) makes the climb enumerate more distinct members than $S$
contains. Contradiction; so a maximal element exists.
$\blacksquare$

**Theorem (Zorn implies well-ordering).** Every set admits a
well-ordering.

*Proof.* For a set $X$, let $S$ be the set of all pairs $(Y, <_Y)$
where $Y \subseteq X$ and $<_Y$ well-orders $Y$ (nonempty: singletons,
and $\varnothing$). Order $S$ by: $(Y, <_Y) \leq (Y', <_{Y'})$ when
$Y \subseteq Y'$, the orders agree on $Y$, and every element of $Y'
\setminus Y$ comes after every element of $Y$. Every chain in $S$ has
an upper bound: the union of the chain's sets, ordered by the union of
the chain's orders (comparability within the chain makes this a
well-ordering: any nonempty subset of the union sits inside one member
of the chain, which is well-ordered). Zorn delivers a maximal
$(M, <_M)$. If $M \neq X$, pick $x \in X \setminus M$ and append it
after all of $M$, a strictly larger well-ordering, contradicting
maximality. So $M = X$: $X$ is well-ordered. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (well-ordering implies choice).** If every set can be
well-ordered, then every family of nonempty sets has a choice
function.

*Proof.* Well-order the union of the family; define the choice
function to pick, from each set in the family, its least member in
that well-ordering (least exists: the set is nonempty and inherits the
well-ordering). $\blacksquare$

**The honest cost.** Choice purchases the basis theorem (Stage F), the
maximal ideal theorem (Stage L), and Tychonoff's theorem (Stage H),
each of which the map shows spending it. It also purchases theorems
that offend intuition, of which the Banach-Tarski decomposition is the
famous specimen. The course adopts choice because the working
mathematics of the later stages spends it at every turn, and because
the axiom table keeps the purchase visible.

**The circle of equivalents, one engine per implication:**

| From | To | The proof's engine |
|---|---|---|
| choice | Zorn's lemma | choice-selected strict upper bounds, climbed by transfinite recursion |
| Zorn's lemma | well-ordering | Zorn applied to the poset of well-ordered subsets of $X$ |
| well-ordering | choice | pick each set's least member in a well-ordering of the union |

Adopting one adopts all three; the course adopts choice and flags every
use.

:::note[Quick check]

1. State the axiom of choice, and name its two proved equivalents.
2. What is a chain in a partially ordered set?
3. What does Zorn's proof climb with, and what stops the climb?
4. Why does the union of a chain of well-orderings remain
   well-ordered?
5. Name two later-stage theorems that spend choice, and one theorem
   that shows its cost.
6. State the shoes-and-socks contrast: which is choice-free, and why?
7. In the well-ordering proof, what would go wrong if Zorn delivered
   only an element bounded above some chain rather than a maximal one?
8. Which of the three implications in this section used transfinite
   recursion, and what did the recursion climb with?

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">
1. Every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function; equivalents: Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering principle.
2. A subfamily whose members are pairwise comparable.
3. The climb uses choice-selected strict upper bounds at every ordinal position; the climb is stopped by the set-size barrier (it outruns the set).
4. Any nonempty subset of the union lies within one member of the chain, which is well-ordered, so it has a least member.
5. Spend: the basis theorem (Stage F), maximal ideals (Stage L), Tychonoff (Stage H). Cost: Banach-Tarski.
6. Shoes: choice-free, because "pick the left one" is a defining rule. Socks: choice is needed, because an arbitrary family of indistinguishable pairs offers no rule, so the existence of a simultaneous selection must be asserted.
7. Nothing would force the element to cover $X$: a chain-bounded element can still miss members of $X$, and the append-one-point contradiction (the engine of maximality) would have nothing to contradict.
8. Choice implies Zorn used transfinite recursion: the climb appends choice-selected strict upper bounds at successor positions and chain-upper-bounds at limit positions, until it outruns the set.
</div>
</details>

:::

## Problems

1. Prove that the negative cut $-\alpha$ of Section 2 is a cut, and
   that $\alpha + (-\alpha) = 0^*$ by the element chase indicated in
   the section.
   *(Hint: for the identity, show every element of $0^*$ is a sum
   $r + s$ with $r \in \alpha$, $s \notin \alpha$; density picks such
   $s$ for every $r$ and Problem 1's own case analysis bounds the
   pairings.)*
2. Prove that every positive real has a square root: for $x > 0$,
   define $\alpha := \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q < 0 \text{ or } q \times q
   < x \text{ on rationals}\}$ and show $\alpha$ is a cut with
   $\alpha \times \alpha = x^*$.
   *(Hint: mirror the $\sqrt{2}$ proof of Section 2; the no-greatest-
   element condition needs the explicit slightly-larger rational
   construction.)*
3. Prove that the decimal expansion of $1/3$ is
   $0.333\ldots$ by the remainder-pigeonhole argument, and that the
   expansion is repeating with period $1$.
   *(Hint: the remainders of $10^k \times 1$ upon division by $3$ are
   $1, 1, 1, \ldots$; apply Stage B's remainder theorem and Section
   3's repeating-means-rational theorem in reverse.)*
4. Prove: the set of all subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is uncountable, using
   the bijection between subsets and their characteristic functions
   into $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, by a diagonal argument on the
   functions.
   *(Hint: given any list $f_0, f_1, \ldots$ of functions $\mathbb{N}
   \to \{0, 1\}$, define $g(n) := 1 - f_n(n)$ and check $g$ differs
   from each $f_k$ at $k$; this is Stage A's power-set diagonal in
   function clothing.)*
5. Use Zorn's lemma to prove: every set $X$ admits a well-ordering,
   by applying Zorn to the poset of well-ordered subsets as in
   Section 6, writing out the three checks (nonempty, chains have
   upper bounds, the maximal element covers $X$) in full.
   *(Hint: the union of a chain of well-orderings is well-ordered
   because any nonempty subset of the union lives inside one member of
   the chain; the maximality argument is the append-one-point
   contradiction.)*

**The Defect.** Stage D built you the real line, and algebra immediately
asks for more than the line contains. The equation $x \times x + 1 = 0$
has no real solution: on the ordered line, every square is $\geq 0$, so
$x \times x = -1$ is impossible (Section 3 of Stage C's crisis, now a
permanent feature rather than a surprise). The naive conjectures: invent
a root ad hoc whenever one is needed, or declare such equations
meaningless. Both fail the same way: algebra wants *systems*, so you need
not just one root of one equation but a closed arithmetic in which
polynomial questions have polynomial answers. Stage E builds that
system in three moves: polynomials rebuilt as formal objects, a new
number constructed as pairs with a forced multiplication rule, and the
fundamental theorem of algebra *declared*: the course map's ledger
opens its longest debt, with Stage K named as the payee, roughly forty
chapters later.

**The One-Line Reveal.** <span class="wn-spoiler-inline" tabindex="0">A
polynomial is its coefficient sequence, not its graph; a number is its
arithmetic, not its size; and the fundamental theorem of algebra is the
promise that the pair-built system you construct in this stage is the
last system algebra will ever demand, a promise proved in Stage K and
spent in every structural stage between.</span>

*The blur is deliberate: form your own reading of the page first, then
click it.*

**Scope.** Consumes Stage D (the real line, its order, the crisis
theorem) and Stage B (arithmetic, induction, division with remainder)
and Stage C (the integers, $\mathbb{Z}/2$, well-definedness method).
Declares exactly one debt: the **fundamental theorem of algebra**
(Section 3), discharged by Stage K3. Formal witnesses pause: the
algebra of this stage lives in Mathlib's commutative-ring machinery,
and importing a library that size for three boxes fails the
proportionality test. The prose proofs stand alone.

## 1. Polynomials as Formal Objects

**The naive conjecture.** A polynomial *is* its function: the object
and the rule that evaluates it are the same thing. Stage C built
$\mathbb{Z}/2$ (Section 5), and it refutes this in a two-element world:
on $\{[0], [1]\}$, the polynomial $x \times x + x$ evaluates to $[0]$
at both elements ($0 \times 0 + 0 = [0]$ and $1 \times 1 + 1 = [1] +
[1] = [0]$ in $\mathbb{Z}/2$): the *same function* as the zero
polynomial. Yet one has degree 2 and the other degree 0: they are
different objects with identical behaviour. A polynomial must
therefore be something whose identity is *syntactic*: the coefficients,
not its evaluated output.

**Definition (polynomial).** A **polynomial** over a number system $R$
is a finite sequence of coefficients from $R$: $(a_0, a_1, \ldots,
a_n)$. The **degree** of a nonzero polynomial is the largest index with
$a_k \neq 0$. The zero polynomial has no degree (convention: degree
$-\infty$, and it is not the degree of any natural number).

**Definition (evaluation).** The value of $(a_0, \ldots, a_n)$ at $x$
is $a_0 + a_1 \times x + \dots + a_n \times x^n$, computed efficiently
by **Horner's scheme**: $\left(\ldots\left((a_n \times x + a_{n-1})
\times x + a_{n-2}\right) \times x \dots\right) + a_0$. Evaluation is a
*separate map* from sequences to the number system, and the separation
that the naive conjecture denied.

**Formal witness (the representation, certified).** The polynomial as a
coefficient list, with Horner evaluation, in core Lean: both facts
hold *by definition* (`rfl`), which is the point: the representation is
the object.

```lean
def evalPoly (coef : List Nat) (x : Nat) : Nat :=
  match coef with
  | [] => 0
  | a :: rest => a + x * evalPoly rest x

theorem eval_nil_w (x : Nat) : evalPoly [] x = 0 := rfl

theorem eval_cons_w (a : Nat) (coef : List Nat) (x : Nat) :
    evalPoly (a :: coef) x = a + x * evalPoly coef x := rfl
```

*Gloss.* The empty coefficient list is the zero polynomial (evaluates
to $0$ everywhere), and prepending a coefficient $a$ shifts the rest up
by one power: `a + x * (rest evaluated at x)`.

**Definition (formal arithmetic).** Addition adds coefficient-wise:
$(a_k) + (b_k) := (a_k + b_k)$. Multiplication is **convolution**: the
coefficient of $x^k$ in a product is $\sum_{i + j = k} a_i \times b_j$
: exactly what expanding $(a_0 + a_1 x + \dots)(b_0 + b_1 x + \dots)$
and collecting powers of $x$ produces.

**Theorem (degree of a product).** Over an integral domain (Stage C's
$\mathbb{Z}$ qualifies: no zero divisors, Section 5's Problem 5), the
degree of a product is the sum of the degrees.

*Proof.* Let $f$ have degree $m$ (leading coefficient $a_m \neq 0$)
and $g$ have degree $n$ (leading coefficient $b_n \neq 0$). The
coefficient of $x^{m + n}$ in $f \times g$ is $a_m \times b_n$ plus
terms $a_i \times b_j$ with $i + j = m + n$ and ($i < m$ or $j < n$).
If $i < m$, then $a_i = 0$; if $j < n$, then $b_j = 0$. So every other
term vanishes and $a_m \times b_n \neq 0$ (no zero divisors). The
product has degree $m + n$. $\blacksquare$

**Quick check.**

1. Write the coefficient sequences of $3 + 0 \times x + 5 \times x^2$
   and of $x$.
2. Compute the convolution coefficient of $x^1$ for
   $(1, 2) \times (3, 4)$.
3. Why does the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ example refute "a polynomial is its
   function"?
4. State the degree-of-a-product theorem, and name the property of
   the coefficient system it consumes.
5. Compute $(1, 2) \times (3, 4)$ completely (all coefficients).
6. Evaluate the coefficient sequence $(2)$ at $x = 5$, and connect it
   to the constant polynomial $2$.
7. Compute the convolution of $(1, 1)$ with $(1, 1)$, and name the
   Stage B counting objects the coefficients $1, 2, 1$ recall.
8. Why does the zero polynomial have *no degree* rather than degree
   $0$, given the leading-coefficient definition?

*Answers:* **1.** $(3, 0, 5)$ and $(0, 1)$. **2.**
$\sum_{i+j=1} a_i b_j = a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 = 1 \times 4 + 2 \times 3 =
10$. **3.** On $\mathbb{Z}/2$ they define the same function but have
different degrees: identity is syntactic (coefficients), not
behavioural. **4.** $\deg(f \times g) = \deg f + \deg g$, consuming no
zero divisors. **5.** Coefficient of $x^0$: $3$; of $x^1$: $4 + 6 =
10$; of $x^2$: $8$. So $(3, 10, 8)$: check by expanding $(1 + 2x)(3 + 4x) = 3 + 10x + 8x^2$.

## 2. The Complex Numbers: Pairs with a Forced Rule

**The wall.** Over $\mathbb{R}$, the polynomial $x \times x + 1$ has no
root: on the ordered line, $x \times x \geq 0$, so $x \times x + 1
\geq 1$ (Section 3 of Stage C proved the stronger fact that even over
$\mathbb{Q}$ no root exists). The naive conjectures: there is no
answer, or the answer is "undefined". Both refuse to build.

**The repair (forced, not invented).** Declare a new object $i$ with
exactly one law: $i \times i = -1$. Demand that $i$ live inside an
arithmetic with the laws you already trust (associativity,
commutativity, distributivity, every real $r$ embedded). Then the
multiplication rule is *forced*: $(a + i \times b) \times (c + i
\times d) = a \times c + a \times i \times d + i \times b \times c +
i \times i \times b \times d = (a \times c - b \times d) + i \times (a
\times d + b \times c)$. Every choice except $i \times i = -1$ in the
fourth term violates the laws you demanded.

**Definition (the complex numbers).** $\mathbb{C} := \mathbb{R}
\times \mathbb{R}$ with

- $(a, b) + (c, d) := (a + c, b + d)$;
- $(a, b) \times (c, d) := (a \times c - b \times d, a \times d + b
  \times c)$;
- $i := (0, 1)$, and $i \times i = (-1, 0) = -1$: the defining law,
  recovered from the rule.

**Theorem (the naive alternative is broken).** Componentwise
multiplication, $(a, b) \times (c, d) := (a \times c, b \times d)$,
produces zero divisors: the nonzero pair $(1, 0)$ times the nonzero
pair $(0, 1)$ is $(0, 0)$.

*Proof.* Direct substitution. And zero divisors destroy
cancellation: $x \times (1, 0) = y \times (1, 0)$ with $(x, y) =
(0, 1)$-pairs cannot cancel, so equations stop being solvable by the
course's standard moves. The forced rule exists precisely to avoid
this. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem (ℂ is a field).** Every nonzero $(a, b)$ has a
multiplicative inverse: $(a, b)^{-1} = \left(\frac{a}{a^2 + b^2},
\frac{-b}{a^2 + b^2}\right)$, the denominators being nonzero because
$a^2 + b^2 = 0$ over $\mathbb{R}$ forces $a = b = 0$.

*Proof.* Compute the product: $(a, b) \times \left(\frac{a}{a^2+b^2},
\frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right) = \left(\frac{a^2 + b^2}{a^2 + b^2},
\frac{-a \times b + a \times b}{a^2 + b^2}\right) = (1, 0)$, the
multiplicative identity. Every component law used is Stage D's or
Stage B's. $\blacksquare$

**Definition (conjugation, modulus).** The **conjugate** of $(a, b)$
is $(a, -b)$, written $\overline{(a, b)}$; the **modulus** is
$|(a, b)| := \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ (Stage D's square-root theorem makes
this a real number for every pair).

**Theorem (conjugation facts).** $\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} +
\overline{w}$; $\overline{z \times w} = \overline{z} \times
\overline{w}$; $z \times \overline{z} = |z|^2$ as a real; and $z
\times \overline{z} = 0 \to z = 0$.

*Proof.* The first two are direct expansions. For the third: $z
\times \overline{z} = (a^2 + b^2, 0)$ for $z = (a, b)$ (multiply out),
whose first component is $a^2 + b^2$ (the modulus squared) and
whose second is $0$. If $z \times \overline{z} = 0$, then $a^2 + b^2
= 0$ over $\mathbb{R}$, which forces $a = b = 0$ (squares are
nonnegative, Stage D), so $z = 0$. $\blacksquare$

**Quick check.**

1. Compute $(2, 3) \times (1, -1)$ by the forced rule.
2. Show $i \times i = -1$ from the rule.
3. Compute the inverse of $(3, 4)$ and verify the product is $(1, 0)$.
4. Where exactly does the componentwise alternative break the course's
   standard moves?
5. Compute $\overline{(2, -3)}$ and $(2, -3) \times \overline{(2,
   -3)}$.
6. Prove $\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} + \overline{w}$ from the
   rule.
7. Why is the modulus well-defined (not just "take a root")?
8. Which Stage D theorem is consumed by the definition of the
   modulus?
9. Compute $(1, 2) \times (4, -3)$ by the forced rule.
10. Prove $\overline{\overline{z}} = z$ from Section 2's conjugation
    definition.
11. Compute $i^{3}$ and $i^{4}$ from $i \times i = -1$, and state
    the pattern.
12. Why does $a^2 + b^2 = 0$ over $\mathbb{R}$ force $a = b = 0$,
    and where was this fact proved?

*Answers:* **1.** $(2 \times 1 - 3 \times (-1), 2 \times (-1) + 3
\times 1) = (5, 1)$. **2.** $(0, 1) \times (0, 1) = (0 - 1, 0 + 0) =
(-1, 0)$. **3.** Inverse $= \left(\frac{3}{25}, \frac{-4}{25}\right)$;
product $= \left(\frac{9 + 16}{25}, \frac{12 - 12}{25}\right) = (1,
0)$. **4.** Zero divisors: cancellation (Problem-style moves
throughout Stage B and C) fails. **5.** $(2, 3)$ and the product is
$(4 + 9, 0) = (13, 0)$: the modulus squared as a real. **6.**
Componentwise addition commutes componentwise. **7.** Stage D's
square-root theorem: every positive real has a square root, so the
$\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ exists and is unique. **8.** The square-root
theorem (Section 2 of Stage D): the crisis resolved.

## 3. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: Declared

**The theorem (declaration).** Every nonconstant polynomial with
complex coefficients has at least one complex root: for every $f$ of
degree $\geq 1$, there exists $z \in \mathbb{C}$ with $f(z) = 0$. By
repeated division (Stage E's own convolution and Stage 1's evaluation),
this is equivalent to: every polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ factors
completely into linear factors.

**Why this is a declaration, not a derivation.** The proof history is
two centuries long: Euler failed; d'Alembert's 1746 proof had a gap
filled only with analysis beyond his tools; Gauss gave four proofs
across his career, his first (1799) also containing a gap later
filled; the modern proofs require either the completeness of
$\mathbb{R}$ (Stage D) driving a topological argument, or complex
analysis itself (Stage K's residue theory gives the shortest proof).
Every route consumes machinery this course has not yet built, or is
building in Stage K. Declaring the theorem with a named payee is the
ledger being honest: the course uses the truth, and Stage K pays it.
(The ledger's other entries (the recursion principle, choice) follow
the same shape.)

**What the declaration licenses downstream.** With every complex
polynomial splitting into linear factors:

- **Eigenvalues always exist**: Stage F's characteristic polynomial of
  any complex-linear operator has a root, so eigenvector chains never
  dead-end (Stage F's eigenvector chapter consumes this).
- **Every polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with
  multiplicity**: the factorization $f = c \times \prod (x - z_k)$
  gives them directly.
- **Real polynomials factor into real linear and quadratic factors**:
  nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs (conjugation respects real
  coefficients and roots, Section 2's conjugation facts), and each
  conjugate pair contributes a real quadratic factor (Problem 4).
- **Algebraic closedness of ℂ**: no further number system is ever
  needed for polynomial equations: the reason ℂ and not something
  beyond ℂ appears in the course map's promise.

**Ponder.** Before reading on: the declaration says Stage K will prove
this using complex analysis, a theory of *differentiating* functions
like $z \mapsto z^2 + 1$. Why would differentiation be the tool for a
theorem about roots? Attempt a one-sentence guess before revealing.

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Compare your guess</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

The shortest proof assumes $f$ has *no* root and derives a
contradiction: if $f$ never vanishes, then $1/f$ is a well-behaved
(whole, bounded-away-from-zero) function; but complex
differentiability is so rigid that a whole, bounded function must be
constant (Liouville's consequence, Stage K), and $1/f$ constant forces
$f$ constant, contradicting nonconstant. The rigidity of
differentiation is the engine: roots are unavoidable because
avoiding them makes functions too tame to exist. The course's Stage K
builds exactly enough rigidity to run this.

</div>
</details>

**Quick check.**

1. State the fundamental theorem of algebra in root form and in
   factor form.
2. How many roots does a degree-$n$ polynomial have, counted how?
3. Why do nonreal roots of real polynomials come in pairs? (Section
   2's conjugation facts.)
4. What does each conjugate pair contribute to the real
   factorization?
5. Which stage pays the declaration, and with which tool?
6. What does the declaration license for Stage F?
7. Name the rigidity consequence Stage K's proof consumes.
8. Why is declaring with a named payee honest, per the ledger's
   design?

*Answers:* **1.** Root form: every nonconstant $f$ over $\mathbb{C}$
has some $z$ with $f(z) = 0$; factor form: $f$ factors completely
into linear factors. **2.** Exactly $n$, counted with multiplicity.
**3.** Conjugation maps roots of real-coefficient polynomials to
roots: $\overline{f(z)} = f(\overline{z})$. **4.** A real quadratic
$(x - z)(x - \overline{z})$. **5.** Stage K, by Liouville-style
rigidity of complex differentiation. **6.** Eigenvalues exist for
every complex-linear operator: the characteristic polynomial always
splits. **7.** A whole, bounded function is constant (Liouville's
consequence). **8.** The ledger bans silent assumptions: an undeclared
use of an unproved theorem is exactly the failure mode the two-ledger
design exists to prevent.

## Stage Gate

:::caution[Pass mark: four of five]
Before the structural stages, answer these five without notes. A failed
gate names the section to reread (1: Section 1; 2: Section 2; 3:
Section 3; 4 and 5: the declaration and its consequences).

1. State the formal-object definition of a polynomial, and the
   $\mathbb{Z}/2$ refutation of "a polynomial is its function".
2. State the forced multiplication rule, and derive $i \times i$ from
   it.
3. Prove: every nonzero complex number has an inverse.
4. State the fundamental theorem of algebra in both forms.
5. Name the declaration's payee, the tool of its future proof, and
   two consequences it licenses.

<details class="wn-spoiler">
<summary>Gate answers</summary>
<div class="wn-spoiler-body">

**1.** A polynomial is a finite coefficient sequence; on
$\mathbb{Z}/2$, $x \times x + x$ and the zero polynomial define the
same function but have different degrees: identity is syntactic.
**2.** $(a, b) \times (c, d) := (a \times c - b \times d, a \times d + b \times c)$; $i \times i = (0, 1) \times (0, 1) = (-1, 0) = -1$.
**3.** $(a, b)^{-1} = \left(\frac{a}{a^2 + b^2}, \frac{-b}{a^2 +
b^2}\right)$; the product is $(1, 0)$ by direct expansion. **4.**
Root form: every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root;
factor form: complete splitting into linear factors. **5.** Stage K3
pays it, with the rigidity of complex differentiation (Liouville's
consequence); it licenses eigenvalue existence (Stage F) and the
$n$-roots-with-multiplicity count, hence conjugate-pair real
factorizations.

</div>
</details>

:::

## Problems

**Problems.** The quick checks tested recall. These chain several
results and require full written arguments.

1. Prove the **convolution formula** for multiplication: expanding
   $(a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_m x^m)(b_0 + b_1 x + \dots + b_n x^n)$
   with Stage B's distributivity and collecting powers of $x$, show
   the coefficient of $x^k$ is $\sum_{i + j = k} a_i \times b_j$.
   *(Hint: each product term $a_i x^i \times b_j x^j$ contributes to
   exactly one power, $i + j$; group the terms by that power.)*
2. Prove **conjugation respects polynomials with real coefficients**:
   for $f$ with real coefficients, $\overline{f(z)} = f(\overline{z})$
   (induction on the degree, using conjugation's respect for $+$ and
   $\times$). Conclude: if $z$ is a root of a real $f$, so is
   $\overline{z}$.
   *(Hint: conjugation distributes over sums and products (Section
   2's facts.)*
3. Prove: a real quadratic with a nonreal root $z$ factors as $(x -
   z)(x - \overline{z})$ with *real* coefficients, and compute it for
   $z = (0, 1)$-root of $x^2 + 1$.
   *(Hint: the coefficients are $-2 \times \mathrm{Re}(z)$ and
   $|z|^2$, both real by construction.)*
4. Prove: a degree-$n$ polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has **at most**
   $n$ roots (distinct), using Stage E's degree-of-a-product theorem
   and induction: if $z_1$ is a root, divide $f$ by $(x - z_1)$ (Stage
   1's formal division) and show the quotient has degree $n
   \ominus 1$.
   *(Hint: the division step is the factor theorem, proved by
   evaluating the quotient form $f = (x - z_1) \times q + r$ at
   $z_1$.)*
5. Use the declaration + Problem 4 to prove: every degree-$n$
   polynomial over $\mathbb{C}$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with
   multiplicity.
   *(Hint: induction combining "at most $n$ distinct" with "at least
   $n$ counted with multiplicity" from the complete splitting; the
   distinct-count is at most the multiplicity-count.)*

## Stage G Euclidean Analysis
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/17-core-course/stage-g-euclidean-analysis/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">

  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "mathematics", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "17 Core Course", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/17-core-course"}, {"name": "Stage G: Euclidean Analysis", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/17-core-course/stage-g-euclidean-analysis"}]
