</script>

School mathematics is calibrated to an exam. Different boards examine different
subsets, in different notation, at different depths; and every one of them
leaves the same gaps, because a timed paper cannot test whether you *understand*
what a limit is, only whether you can compute one. University mathematics is the
opposite: it assumes you know what the objects are, and examines whether you can
prove things about them.

This page closes the gap. It defines every term the first-year tracks use,
proves every rule it states, and tells you explicitly which parts of school
mathematics to keep, which to unlearn, and which to upgrade. **If you are
confident, skim it and take the self-test in the last section; if any answer
surprises you, read the section it came from.** Nothing here reappears as an
exam topic; it is the foundation the tracks stand on, and the tracks link back
here the first time they use a term.

The order is by dependency, not by difficulty. Section 1 is logic, because
every proof technique is a logical move with a name. Sections 2–3 are sets and
functions, because the whole of the university course is about maps between
structured sets. Section 4 is proof technique. Sections 5–8 are the school
topics rebuilt rigorously: algebra, trigonometry, geometry, and calculus.

## Intuition

School mathematics teaches *procedures*: differentiate this, solve that,
complete the square. University mathematics studies *objects*: functions,
spaces, maps between them, and the theorems they obey. The transition is the
shift from "what is the answer" to "why is this true", and the reason it trips
people up is not difficulty but vocabulary; university mathematics names the
moves school mathematics performs silently.

A limit is the first example. At school, $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ is
a fact to use. At university it is a *definition* -
$\forall\varepsilon > 0\ \exists\delta > 0 : 0 < |x| < \delta \Rightarrow \left|\frac{\sin x}{x} - 1\right| < \varepsilon$; and once the definition is
available, "prove that the limit is 1" becomes a different kind of task, one
that needs the squeeze theorem and the geometry of the unit circle. This page
gives you both layers for every object below: the definition, and the school
result it recovers.

## 1. Logic: the grammar of proof

**Definition (statement).** A **statement** (or proposition) is a declarative
sentence that is either true or false. "7 is prime" is a statement; "is 7
prime?" and "$x + 1 = 5$" are not; the last is an *open* statement, true for
some $x$ and false for others.

**Connectives.** Given statements $P$ and $Q$:

<div class="table-wrap">

| symbol | name | true when |
| ------ | ---- | --------- |
| $\neg P$ | negation ("not") | $P$ is false |
| $P \wedge Q$ | conjunction ("and") | both true |
| $P \vee Q$ | disjunction ("or") | at least one true; *inclusive* or |
| $P \Rightarrow Q$ | implication ("if…then") | $P$ false, or $Q$ true |

</div>

<div class="table-wrap">

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P \Rightarrow Q$ |
| --- | --- | ----------------- |
| T   | T   | T                 |
| T   | F   | **F**             |
| F   | T   | T                 |
| F   | F   | T                 |

</div>

The two rows that surprise people are the last two: a false hypothesis makes an
implication *vacuously true*. "If $2 + 2 = 5$ then I am the Pope" is a true
statement. This is not a trick; it is what makes proofs by contradiction and
empty-set arguments work.

**Definition (converse, contrapositive).** For $P \Rightarrow Q$: the
**converse** is $Q \Rightarrow P$; the **contrapositive** is
$\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$.

**Proposition.** An implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.
An implication and its converse are not.

*Proof.* Build the truth table. $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ is false exactly
when $\neg Q$ is true and $\neg P$ false, i.e. $Q$ false and $P$ true; the
single row where $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false. For the converse,
$Q \Rightarrow P$ is false when $Q$ true, $P$ false; a different row, so the
converse has a different truth table from the original. $\blacksquare$

**Why this matters.** Mixing up a statement with its converse is the most common
logical error in mathematics. "If $x = 2$ then $x^2 = 4$" is true; its converse
"if $x^2 = 4$ then $x = 2$" is false ($x = -2$). Convergent sequences have
bounded terms; *bounded* terms do not give convergence.

**Quantifiers.** $\forall$ ("for all") and $\exists$ ("there exists").

$$
\forall\varepsilon > 0\ \exists\delta > 0 : P(\delta) \quad\text{means}\quad
\text{for each }\varepsilon,\text{ a }\delta\text{ may be chosen (possibly depending on it).}
$$

**Proposition (negation rules).** $\neg\forall x\,P(x) \equiv \exists x\,\neg P(x)$
and $\neg\exists x\,P(x) \equiv \forall x\,\neg P(x)$. Quantifiers negate in
order, and $\forall$ becomes $\exists$.

*Why this matters.* The negation of "the sequence converges" -
$\forall\varepsilon > 0\ \exists N\ \forall n \geq N : |a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ -
is "the sequence does not converge":
$\exists\varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n \geq N : |a_n - L| \geq \varepsilon$.
Every "prove this does not converge" exercise is that string, applied.

## 2. Sets

**Definition.** A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, its **elements**.
$x \in A$ means $x$ is an element; $A \subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ is
an element of $B$.

**Definition.** For sets $A, B$ in a universe $U$:

$$
A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}, \quad
A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}, \quad
A^c = \{x \in U : x \notin A\},
$$

$$
A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A, b \in B\}, \quad
A \setminus B = \{x \in A : x \notin B\}.
$$

**Proposition (De Morgan).** $(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$.

*Proof.* $x \in (A\cup B)^c$ iff $x \notin A \cup B$ iff $x \notin A$ and
$x \notin B$ iff $x \in A^c$ and $x \in B^c$. $\blacksquare$

**Definition (function).** See Section 3; but note the notation for images and
preimages: $f(A) = \{f(a) : a \in A\}$ and $f^{-1}(B) = \{x : f(x) \in B\}$.
The preimage *always* exists for any $B$; the inverse function may not.

**Definition (cardinality, finite and countable).** Two sets are
**equipotent** if there is a bijection between them. A set is **countable** if
it is equipotent to a subset of $\mathbb{N}$; **countably infinite** if to
$\mathbb{N}$ itself; **uncountable** otherwise.

**Theorem (Cantor).** $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable; $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.

*Proof for $\mathbb{Q}$.* List fractions by increasing $p + q$ for $p/q$ in
lowest terms with $q > 0$; each positive rational appears exactly once, and the
list is infinite, so $\mathbb{Q}^+ \sim \mathbb{N}$; reflect to include
negatives and zero.

*Proof for $\mathbb{R}$ (Cantor's diagonal).* Suppose
$\mathbb{R} \sim \mathbb{N}$ via a list $r_1, r_2, \dots$ of reals in $(0,1)$,
each with decimal expansion $0.d_{n1}d_{n2}d_{n3}\dots$. Construct
$d = 0.e_1e_2e_3\dots$ with $e_n = 5$ if $d_{nn} \neq 5$ and $e_n = 6$ if
$d_{nn} = 5$. Then $d \in (0,1)$ and $d \neq r_n$ for every $n$; it differs
from $r_n$ in the $n$-th decimal; contradicting the list's completeness.
(Avoiding dual expansions like $0.4999\ldots = 0.5$: the digit choice $5/6$
never produces a trailing $9$.) $\blacksquare$

The theorem to internalise: *infinity has sizes*. The rationals are dense but
countable; the reals are uncountable. Measure theory; the foundation of
probability; is built on exactly this distinction.

## 3. Functions

**Definition.** A **function** $f : A \to B$ is a rule assigning to each
$a \in A$ exactly one $f(a) \in B$. $A$ is the domain, $B$ the codomain, and
$f(A)$ the image.

**Definition.** $f$ is **injective** ($f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2$),
**surjective** ($f(A) = B$), and **bijective** if both.

**Proposition.** $f : A \to B$ is bijective iff it has an inverse
$f^{-1} : B \to A$ with $f^{-1}(f(a)) = a$ and $f(f^{-1}(b)) = b$.

*Proof.* If $f$ is bijective, define $f^{-1}(b) = a$ where $a$ is the unique
element with $f(a) = b$; unique by injectivity, existing by surjectivity. The
two compositions are identities by construction. Conversely, if $f^{-1}$
exists, injectivity and surjectivity follow from the two composition
identities. $\blacksquare$

**Definition (composition).** $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$, defined where
$f(x) \in$ domain of $g$. Composition is associative -
$(h \circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f)$; and *not* commutative.

**Proposition.** $(g \circ f)$ injective $\Rightarrow$ $f$ injective.

*Proof.* $f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2)) \Rightarrow (g\circ f)(a_1) = (g \circ f)(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2$ by injectivity of
$g \circ f$. Note $g$ itself need not be injective. $\blacksquare$

Functions are the objects of university mathematics: every structure; a group,
a metric space, a measure; comes with the class of functions that preserve it.
The vocabulary here (injective, surjective, bijective, inverse, composition) is
the vocabulary of every definition that follows.

## 4. Proof techniques

**Direct proof.** Assume $P$; derive $Q$ by a chain of implications.

**Proof by contrapositive.** To prove $P \Rightarrow Q$, prove
$\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$. Used when the contrapositive gives more to work
with: proving "$n^2$ even $\Rightarrow n$ even" is easiest as
"$n$ odd $\Rightarrow n^2$ odd", since "odd" has a usable form ($n = 2k+1$).

**Proof by contradiction.** Assume $P$ and $\neg Q$; derive any falsehood.
The irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ is the classic:

*Proof.* Suppose $\sqrt{2} = p/q$ in lowest terms. Then $p^2 = 2q^2$, so $p^2$
is even, so $p$ is even; write $p = 2k$. Then $4k^2 = 2q^2$, so $q^2 = 2k^2$,
so $q$ is even too. Both even contradicts lowest terms. $\blacksquare$

Note the lemma it used; "$p^2$ even $\Rightarrow p$ even"; which itself
needs the contrapositive form above. Proofs are layered.

**Proof by cases.** Partition and prove each part: "even $n$" and "odd $n$".

**Proof by induction.** To prove $S(n)$ for all $n \geq n_0$: prove $S(n_0)$
(base) and $S(n) \Rightarrow S(n+1)$ (inductive step).

*Proof that it works (well-ordering principle).* Suppose some $S(n)$ fails; let
$n^*$ be the least such; it exists because $\mathbb{N}$ is well-ordered. Then
$n^* > n_0$, so $S(n^* - 1)$ holds, so $S(n^*)$ holds by the inductive step -
contradiction. $\blacksquare$

*Worked example.* Prove $\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

*Base.* $n = 1$: $1 = \frac{1 \cdot 2}{2}$. *Step.* Assume
$\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Then

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n+1} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (n+1) = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2},
$$

which is the formula at $n+1$. $\blacksquare$

**Proof by counterexample.** To disprove $\forall x\,P(x)$, exhibit one $x$ with
$\neg P(x)$. This is the *only* way to disprove a universal statement, and one
counterexample ends the matter; which is why finding them is so valuable.

## 5. Algebra: the school toolkit, upgraded

These are used silently in every proof. Fluency matters: a proof can fail on
algebra.

**Expansion and factorisation.**

$$
(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, \qquad
(a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2, \qquad
a^3 \pm b^3 = (a \pm b)(a^2 \mp ab + b^2).
$$

**The quadratic formula and completing the square.**

$$
ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \iff x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a},
$$

obtained by completing the square; and completing the square is also how you
find the vertex of a parabola and derive the canonical form of any quadratic in
$x$ and $y$.

**Proposition (AM–GM).** For $a, b \geq 0$: $\frac{a+b}{2} \geq \sqrt{ab}$, with
equality iff $a = b$.

*Proof.* $(a - b)^2 \geq 0 \iff a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \geq 0 \iff a^2 + b^2 \geq 2ab \iff \frac{a+b}{2} \geq \sqrt{ab}$
(adding $2ab$ and halving; taking positive square roots). Equality iff
$(a-b)^2 = 0$. $\blacksquare$

**Inequalities you must be able to manipulate.**

- $x < y$ and $c > 0 \Rightarrow cx < cy$; but for $c < 0$ the inequality
  *reverses*. Dividing by a negative without flipping is the most common
  school-level error, and in analysis it proves false theorems.
- Triangle inequality: $|x + y| \leq |x| + |y|$, with equality iff $x, y$ have
  the same sign. Proof: $|x+y|^2 = (x+y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 \leq x^2 + 2|xy| + y^2 = (|x|+|y|)^2$ using $xy \leq |xy|$.
- Reverse triangle: $\big||x| - |y|\big| \leq |x - y|$. Proof: apply the
  triangle inequality to $x = (x - y) + y$ and to $y = (y - x) + x$, then
  combine.

**Proposition (Bernoulli).** For $x > -1$ and $r \in \mathbb{N}$:
$(1+x)^r \geq 1 + rx$.

*Proof.* Induction. Base $r = 1$: equality. Step: assume
$(1+x)^r \geq 1 + rx$. Multiply both sides by the positive $(1+x)$:
$(1+x)^{r+1} \geq (1+rx)(1+x) = 1 + (r+1)x + rx^2 \geq 1 + (r+1)x$.
$\blacksquare$

**Exponentials and logarithms.** $a^x$ and $\log_a x$ are inverse functions;
$\log(xy) = \log x + \log y$; $\log(x^r) = r \log x$. The natural logarithm uses
$e = \lim_{n\to\infty}(1 + 1/n)^n$; a limit, justified rigorously in the
real-analysis track. **$\log$ of a negative number is undefined over the
reals.**

## 6. Trigonometry

**Definition (radian).** An angle of $\theta$ radians subtends an arc of length
$\theta$ on the unit circle. $\pi$ radians $= 180°$. **All calculus assumes
radians**; $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ is false in degrees, because the
derivative of $\sin$ at $0$ is $\pi/180$-ish in degrees and exactly $1$ in
radians.

<div class="table-wrap">

| $\theta$ | $0$ | $\pi/6$ | $\pi/4$ | $\pi/3$ | $\pi/2$ |
| -------- | --- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- |
| $\sin\theta$ | $0$ | $1/2$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos\theta$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $1/2$ | $0$ |
| $\tan\theta$ | $0$ | $1/\sqrt3$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | - |

</div>

**Identities, proved not listed.**

*Pythagoras.* $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$: it is the equation of the unit
circle, since $\cos\theta, \sin\theta$ are its coordinates.

*Angle addition.*

$$
\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta,
\qquad
\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta.
$$

*Proof of the first.* Take points $P = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$ and apply the
rotation through $\beta$, whose matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix}\cos\beta & -\sin\beta\\ \sin\beta & \cos\beta\end{pmatrix}$;
the rotated coordinates are exactly the two formulas, since rotation by $\beta$
maps the unit circle to itself and sends the angle $\alpha$ to $\alpha + \beta$. $\blacksquare$

*Even–odd.* $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$ and $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$:
cosine is even, sine is odd; visible from the unit circle.

*Double angle and the half-angle substitution.* Setting $\alpha = \beta$:
$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$,
$\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta$. Rearranged: $\cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}$ -
the identity every Fourier series computation uses.

**Proposition (the fundamental limits).**
$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ and $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac12$.

*Proof of the first (squeeze theorem).* For $0 < x < \pi/2$, compare areas:
$\triangle OAB \leq \text{sector} \leq \triangle OAC$ gives
$\frac{1}{2}\sin x \leq \frac{x}{2} \leq \frac{1}{2}\tan x$, so

$$
\cos x \leq \frac{\sin x}{x} \leq 1,
$$

and since $\cos x \to 1$, the squeeze theorem (proved in the real-analysis
track from the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition) gives the limit. The second
follows: $\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2 \to \frac{1}{2}$. $\blacksquare$

## 7. Coordinate geometry

**Definition (distance, midpoint, gradient).** In $\mathbb{R}^2$,
$d(P, Q) = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2}$ (Pythagoras); the gradient of
the line through $P, Q$ is $m = \frac{y_1 - y_2}{x_1 - x_2}$.

**Proposition.** Lines $y = m_1x + c_1$ and $y = m_2x + c_2$ are perpendicular
iff $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

*Proof.* A line of gradient $m$ has direction vector $(1, m)$. Two direction
vectors are perpendicular iff their dot product vanishes:
$(1, m_1)\cdot(1, m_2) = 1 + m_1 m_2 = 0$. $\blacksquare$

**Conic sections.** The circle $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$; the parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$; the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$; the hyperbola
$\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$. Each is the slice of a cone, and each
is a level set of a quadratic; which is why completing the square classifies
them all.

**Vectors and the dot product.** $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta$, so $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$ means
perpendicular; the algebraic form of orthogonality that every later course
generalises.

## 8. Single-variable calculus

**Definition (derivative).** $f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$
when the limit exists.

**The standard derivatives, with one proved.**

<div class="table-wrap">

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| ------ | ------- |
| $x^r$ | $rx^{r-1}$ |
| $e^x$ | $e^x$ |
| $\ln x$ | $1/x$ |
| $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ |

</div>

*Proof for $\sin$, the one needing trigonometry.* From the definition and the
angle-addition formula,

$$
\frac{\sin(x+h) - \sin x}{h}
= \sin x\,\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x\,\frac{\sin h}{h}
\to \sin x \cdot 0 + \cos x \cdot 1 = \cos x,
$$

using the two fundamental limits of §6. The factor $h$ in the denominator and
the radians convention are what make this come out clean; which is *why* the
course uses radians. $\blacksquare$

**Rules.** Product: $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$. Quotient:
$\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}$. Chain:
$(g \circ f)'(x) = g'(f(x))\,f'(x)$.

*Proof of the chain rule (with the hypothesis stated).* If $g$ is differentiable
at $f(x)$ and $f$ at $x$, and the difference quotients of $f$ stay bounded away
from zero where needed, then

$$
\frac{g(f(x+h)) - g(f(x))}{h} = \frac{g(f(x+h)) - g(f(x))}{f(x+h) - f(x)}
\cdot \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}.
$$

The subtlety; the denominator $f(x+h) - f(x)$ can be zero for arbitrarily
small $h$; is handled by writing the difference quotient of $g$ as a continuous
function of the increment, which is why the honest proof defines
$\psi(k) = \frac{g(f(x)+k) - g(f(x))}{k}$ for $k \neq 0$ and $\psi(0) = g'(f(x))$,
making $\psi$ continuous. Then $g(f(x+h)) - g(f(x)) = \psi(f(x+h) - f(x))$ holds
*even when the increment is zero*, and the limit factors. $\blacksquare$

**Definition (integral).** $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is the limit of Riemann sums
$\sum f(\xi_i)\,\Delta x_i$ as the mesh goes to zero.

**The fundamental theorem of calculus.** If $f$ is continuous and
$F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, then $F'(x) = f(x)$; and
$\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$ for any antiderivative $F$.

*Proof of the first part.* $\frac{F(x+h) - F(x)}{h} = \frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h}f$,
and by continuity $f$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $f(x)$ on $[x, x+h]$ for small
$h$, so the average is within $\varepsilon$ of $f(x)$. $\blacksquare$

**The school results recovered.** Integration by parts from the product rule -
$(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ integrates to $\int fg' = fg - \int f'g$. Substitution from
the chain rule; $\frac{d}{dx}g(f(x)) = g'(f(x))f'(x)$ read backwards.
Both are *theorems about antiderivatives*, and both fail without the
hypotheses, which is why the derivative table above was proved rather than
listed.

## 9. Notation: the upgrade list

Some school notation is discarded, and using it flags your work:

<div class="table-wrap">

| school | university | why |
| ------ | ---------- | ----- |
| $\sin^2 x$ meaning $(\sin x)^2$ | kept, but $\sin^{-1}x$ means *arcsine*, never $1/\sin x$ | the $^{-1}$ collision |
| "solving for $x$" | "determining the preimage $f^{-1}(\{y\})$" | functions, not puzzles |
| $=$ used loosely | $=$ only for genuine equality; $\approx$, $\to$, $\propto$ as needed | each symbol is a claim |
| implicit domains | domains stated with every function | $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ has domain, and it matters |
| "can't divide by zero" | "$f$ is defined where its denominator is nonzero" | the domain is part of the function |

</div>

**Proof hygiene.** Never write $\Rightarrow$ between two statements you have
not proved connect. Never use the theorem you are proving. State where every
hypothesis is used. If a step says "clearly" and it is not, it is not clear.

## 10. Self-test

Attempt these before track 1. Answers below; each links back to its section.

1. Write the negation of: "for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that
   for all $n \geq N$, $|a_n| < \varepsilon$". (§1)
2. Prove that $f(x) = x^3$ is injective on $\mathbb{R}$. (§3)
3. Prove that $n^3 - n$ is divisible by $6$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. (§4,
   cases + induction)
4. Show $x^2 > x$ for all $x > 1$, and find every $x$ with $x^2 < x$. (§5)
5. Prove $\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta}$,
   stating where the formula fails. (§6)
6. Show the lines $y = 2x + 1$ and $x + 2y = 3$ are perpendicular. (§7)
7. Differentiate $x^x$ for $x > 0$, stating the rule used. (§8, chain + log)
8. Prove $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$ using the fundamental limits. (§8)

**Answers.**

1. $\exists\varepsilon > 0\;\forall N\;\exists n \geq N : |a_n| \geq \varepsilon$.
2. $f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a^3 = b^3 \Rightarrow (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2) = 0$;
   $a^2 + ab + b^2 = (a + b/2)^2 + \frac{3b^2}{4} \geq \frac{3b^2}{4} > 0$ unless
   $a = b = 0$, so $a = b$.
3. $n^3 - n = (n-1)n(n+1)$ is a product of three consecutive integers, so one is
   even and one is a multiple of 3.
4. $x^2 > x \iff x(x-1) > 0 \iff x > 1$ or $x < 0$; $x^2 < x \iff 0 < x < 1$.
5. Divide $\sin(\alpha+\beta)$ by $\cos(\alpha+\beta)$, then divide numerator and
   denominator by $\cos\alpha\cos\beta$; it fails when $\tan\alpha\tan\beta = 1$,
   i.e. when $\alpha + \beta = \pi/2$ and the tangent is undefined.
6. Gradients $2$ and $-1/2$: product $-1$.
7. $x^x = e^{x\ln x}$, so $\frac{d}{dx} = e^{x\ln x}(\ln x + 1) = x^x(\ln x + 1)$;
   chain rule with $f = \ln$ and $g = e^{(\cdot)}$.
8. $\frac{\cos(x+h) - \cos x}{h} = \cos x\,\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} - \sin x\,\frac{\sin h}{h} \to -\sin x$.

## Glossary
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/glossary/

## Algebra

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Limits] --> B[Continuity]
    B --> C[Differentiation]
    C --> D[Integration]
```


**Binomial**: An algebraic expression with two terms, such as (a + b). The binomial theorem provides a formula for expanding (a + b)ⁿ.

**Completing the Square**: A method for solving quadratic equations by rewriting ax² + bx + c in the form a(x - h)² + k. Used to derive the quadratic formula.

**Discriminant**: For a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant is Δ = b² - 4ac. Determines the nature of roots: positive (two real), zero (one repeated), negative (complex).

**Exponent**: The power to which a number is raised. In aⁿ, n is the exponent. Laws include aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ.

**Function**: A relation where each input has exactly one output, written as f(x). The domain is the set of inputs; the range is the set of outputs.

**Inequality**: A mathematical statement comparing two expressions using <, >, ≤, ≥, or ≠. Solutions are intervals or sets of values.

**Linear Equation**: An equation of the form y = mx + c, where m is the slope and c is the y-intercept. Graphs as a straight line.

**Logarithm**: The inverse of exponentiation. log_b(x) = n means bⁿ = x. Properties include log_b(xy) = log_b(x) + log_b(y).

**Matrix**: A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns, denoted [aᵢⱼ]. Used to represent linear transformations and solve systems of equations.

**Polynomial**: An expression consisting of variables and coefficients involving only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and non-negative integer exponents. Degree is the highest power.

**Quadratic Formula**: The solutions to ax² + bx + c = 0 are x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / (2a). Derived from completing the square.

**Quadratic Function**: A polynomial function of degree 2, f(x) = ax² + bx + c. Its graph is a parabola opening upward if a > 0.

**Set**: A well-defined collection of distinct objects, denoted {a, b, c}. Operations include union (∪), intersection (∩), and complement (A').

**System of Equations**: Two or more equations with the same variables. Can be solved by substitution, elimination, or matrix methods.

**Variable**: A symbol representing an unknown quantity in mathematical expressions and equations.

## Calculus

**Antiderivative**: A function F(x) such that F'(x) = f(x). Also called an indefinite integral. Related: [Integral](/glossary/).

**Chain Rule**: The derivative of a composite function: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) · g'(x). Essential for differentiating nested functions.

**Convergence**: A sequence or series approaches a finite limit. The series Σaₙ converges if partial sums approach a finite value.

**Critical Point**: A point where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) is undefined. May be a local maximum, local minimum, or saddle point.

**Derivative**: The instantaneous rate of change of a function: f'(x) = lim[h→0] (f(x+h) - f(x))/h. Represents slope of tangent line.

**Differential Equation**: An equation involving derivatives of a function. Solutions are functions that satisfy the equation. Types: ODE, PDE.

**Differentiation**: The process of finding derivatives. Rules include power rule, product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule.

**Fundamental Theorem of Calculus**: Links differentiation and integration: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a), where F'(x) = f(x).

**Improper Integral**: An integral with infinite limits or discontinuous integrand. Evaluated as a limit: ∫₁^∞ f(x)dx = lim[b→∞] ∫₁ᵇ f(x)dx.

**Indefinite Integral**: The family of antiderivatives: ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C. C is the constant of integration.

**Inflection Point**: A point where the concavity of a function changes. Occurs where f''(x) = 0 or f''(x) is undefined and changes sign.

**Integral**: The limit of a Riemann sum representing the area under a curve: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = lim[n→∞] Σf(xᵢ)Δx. See also [Antiderivative](/glossary/).

**Integration**: The process of finding integrals. Methods include substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, and trigonometric substitution.

**Limit**: The value a function approaches as the input approaches a point: lim[x→c] f(x) = L. Foundation of calculus.

**Local Maximum**: A point where f(x) is greater than all nearby values. Occurs at critical points where f''(x) < 0.

**Local Minimum**: A point where f(x) is less than all nearby values. Occurs at critical points where f''(x) > 0.

**Mean Value Theorem**: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there exists c ∈ (a,b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a).

**Partial Derivative**: The derivative of a multivariable function with respect to one variable, holding others constant. Denoted ∂f/∂x.

**Riemann Sum**: An approximation of an integral using rectangles: Σf(xᵢ*)Δx. As n → ∞, it approaches the exact integral.

**Series**: The sum of a sequence of terms. A convergent series has a finite sum; a divergent series does not.

**Taylor Series**: An infinite series representation of a function: f(x) = Σf⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! · (x-a)ⁿ. Approximates functions near a point.

## Linear Algebra

**Basis**: A set of linearly independent vectors that span a vector space. Every vector in the space can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of basis vectors.

**Column Space**: The set of all linear combinations of a matrix's columns. Equal to the range of the matrix transformation.

**Determinant**: A scalar value computed from a square matrix that indicates whether the matrix is invertible. det(A) = 0 means A is singular.

**Eigenvalue**: A scalar λ such that A**v** = λ**v** for some non-zero vector **v**. Found by solving det(A - λI) = 0.

**Eigenvector**: A non-zero vector **v** that, when multiplied by matrix A, results in a scalar multiple of itself: A**v** = λ**v**.

**Linear Combination**: An expression of the form c₁**v₁** + c₂**v₂** + ... + cₙ**vₙ**, where cᵢ are scalars and **vᵢ** are vectors.

**Linear Independence**: Vectors are linearly independent if no vector can be written as a linear combination of the others. Equivalent to the only solution of c₁**v₁** + ... + cₙ**vₙ** = **0** being all cᵢ = 0.

**Linear Transformation**: A function T: V → W satisfying T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cv) = cT(v). Represented by matrix multiplication.

**Null Space**: The set of all vectors **x** such that A**x** = **0**. A subspace of the domain.

**Rank**: The dimension of the column space (or row space) of a matrix. Equals the number of linearly independent rows or columns.

**Row Space**: The set of all linear combinations of a matrix's rows. Has the same dimension as the column space.

**Scalar Multiplication**: Multiplying a vector by a scalar, scaling its magnitude without changing direction (unless negative).

**Vector Space**: A set of vectors closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication, satisfying eight axioms. Examples include ℝⁿ and function spaces.

**Vector**: A quantity with both magnitude and direction, represented as an ordered tuple of components. Operations include addition and scalar multiplication.

## Analysis

**Cauchy Sequence**: A sequence where terms become arbitrarily close to each other: for all ε > 0, there exists N such that |aₙ - aₘ| < ε for all n, m > N.

**Compactness**: A property of sets where every open cover has a finite subcover. In ℝⁿ, equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem).

**Continuity**: A function f is continuous at a point c if lim[x→c] f(x) = f(c). Intuitively, the function has no jumps or breaks.

**Convergence**: A sequence {aₙ} converges to L if for all ε > 0, there exists N such that |aₙ - L| < ε for all n > N.

**Divergence**: A sequence or series that does not approach a finite limit. May diverge to ±∞ or oscillate.

**Domain**: The set of inputs for which a function is defined.

**Extreme Value Theorem**: A continuous function on a closed interval [a,b] attains both a maximum and minimum value.

**Intermediate Value Theorem**: If f is continuous on [a,b] and k is between f(a) and f(b), there exists c ∈ [a,b] such that f(c) = k.

**L'Hôpital's Rule**: For indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞, lim[f(x)/g(x)] = lim[f'(x)/g'(x)], provided the limit on the right exists.

**Limit Superior**: The largest limit point of a sequence. Also called lim sup. Measures the "long-term" behavior of oscillating sequences.

**Monotonic Sequence**: A sequence that is either entirely non-increasing or non-decreasing. Monotonic bounded sequences converge.

**One-to-One (Injection)**: A function where each output corresponds to exactly one input. f(x₁) = f(x₂) implies x₁ = x₂.

**Onto (Surjection)**: A function where every element in the codomain is the image of at least one element in the domain.

**Sequence**: An ordered list of numbers a₁, a₂, a₃, ... indexed by natural numbers.

**Series**: The sum of a sequence: Σₙ₌₁^∞ aₙ = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + ...

**Topology**: The study of properties preserved under continuous deformations. Deals with open sets, continuity, and connectedness.

## Probability and Statistics

**Bayes' Theorem**: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Relates conditional probabilities and is fundamental to Bayesian inference.

**Combination**: Selection of items where order doesn't matter: C(n,r) = n! / (r!(n-r)!). Also written as "n choose r."

**Conditional Probability**: The probability of event A given event B has occurred: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

**Continuous Distribution**: A probability distribution with a continuous random variable. Defined by a probability density function (PDF).

**Correlation**: A measure of the linear relationship between two variables, ranging from -1 to 1. Correlation does not imply causation.

**Discrete Distribution**: A probability distribution with a discrete random variable. Defined by a probability mass function (PMF).

**Expected Value**: The average value of a random variable: E[X] = ΣxᵢP(xᵢ) for discrete variables.

**Mean**: The arithmetic average of a set of values. For a sample: x̄ = (1/n)Σxᵢ.

**Median**: The middle value when data is ordered. For even sample sizes, the average of the two middle values.

**Normal Distribution**: A bell-shaped continuous distribution: f(x) = (1/σ√(2π))e^(-(x-μ)²/2σ²). Characterized by mean μ and standard deviation σ.

**Permutation**: Arrangement of items where order matters: P(n,r) = n! / (n-r)!.

**Probability**: The likelihood of an event occurring, ranging from 0 to 1. P(A) = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes).

**Random Variable**: A variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a random experiment. Can be discrete or continuous.

**Sample Space**: The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, denoted S.

**Standard Deviation**: The square root of variance: σ = √(Σ(xᵢ - μ)²/N). Measures the spread of data.

**Variance**: The average of squared deviations from the mean: Var(X) = E[(X - μ)²]. Measures dispersion.

## How To Use
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/how-to-use/

## How to Use These Notes

These notes are built around a small number of findings from education research
that are large in effect and robustly replicated. Knowing them changes how you
should read what follows, because several of them contradict what feels
productive.

## 1. Study worked examples before solving problems

The most replicated finding in mathematics education research over the last
forty years is the **worked example effect** (Sweller & Cooper, 1985; Chen,
Kalyuga & Sweller, 2015). Novices who study fully worked solutions learn more,
and learn faster, than novices who attempt the same problems themselves.

The reason is *element interactivity*. Solving a problem by means-ends analysis
forces you to hold in working memory your current state, the goal state, the
differences between them, and candidate moves; all at once. A worked example
shows you each state and the move that gets you to the next one, so the number
of interacting elements collapses. What remains is the schema you were trying
to learn.

So: **read the worked examples first, and read them actively.** Cover the
solution, predict the next step, uncover, check. A worked example you read
passively is worth a fraction of one you interrogate.

## 2. Then solve problems: the expertise reversal

The worked example effect reverses once you are no longer a novice. Kalyuga,
Chandler, Tuovinen and Sweller (2001) found that for learners who already knew
the material, studying worked examples was *worse* than solving problems: the
example adds redundancy, and redundancy costs attention.

Every page here therefore fades from worked examples to completion problems to
bare problems. The point at which you should stop reading examples and start
solving is the point where you can predict the next step correctly most of the
time. That transition is not optional; continuing to study examples after you
have the schema actively slows you down.

## 3. Test yourself; do not reread

**Retrieval practice**; attempting to recall an answer rather than rereading
it; produces far better retention than restudy, an effect large enough that
Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated it among the two most effective techniques
available to learners.

Rereading feels effective because the text becomes familiar. Familiarity is
*not* learning: it is recognition, and recognition does not help you produce a
proof in an exam. The uncomfortable version; closing the notes and trying to
reconstruct the argument; is the one that works.

Each page here opens with **recall prompts**: questions to attempt from memory
*before* reading. Attempting them and failing is not wasted effort; the failure
is what makes the subsequent reading stick.

## 4. Space your practice, and mix topics

The spacing effect is, in Bjork's words, one of the most general and robust
effects in the history of research on learning and memory. Spaced practice beats
massed practice on delayed tests, often by a factor of two, at equal total study
time.

**Interleaving**; mixing problem types rather than blocking them; is the
efficient way to space. It also does something spacing alone does not: it forces
you to *select* the method, which is the part of problem solving that blocked
practice never exercises. Rohrer's work on mathematics practice shows interleaved
practice substantially outperforming blocked practice on delayed tests, while
learners overwhelmingly report the opposite preference.

That mismatch matters. Blocked practice produces rapid gains that feel like
learning and do not survive the week. Interleaved practice feels worse and
produces knowledge that does. **Do not trust your feeling of fluency as a
measure of learning.** Bjork separates *retrieval strength*; how easily
something comes to mind now; from *storage strength*; how durably it is held.
Massed practice inflates the first and does little for the second.

## 5. Intuition first, then rigour, then both

A definition you cannot motivate is a string of symbols. Each page here follows
the same order:

1. **Motivation.** A concrete problem the concept exists to solve.
2. **Intuition.** What it means, in pictures and plain language.
3. **Definition.** Precisely, with the reason for each hypothesis.
4. **Theorem and proof.** With the *idea* of the proof separated from its
   verification, because the idea is what generalises.
5. **Worked examples.** Fully worked, then faded.
6. **Counterexamples.** Where the naive version breaks, and why the hypotheses
   are load-bearing.
7. **Recall prompts and problems.**

Skipping to (3) and (4) is how mathematics is usually examined and almost never
how it is understood. The counterexamples in (6) are the part most notes omit
and most research depends on: knowing that continuity does not imply
differentiability is worth less than knowing *Weierstrass' function* and being
able to say what it does.

## 6. The rigour ladder

Sections are marked so you can see how deep a given page goes:

<div class="table-wrap">

| Mark | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| **F** Foundation | Definitions and first examples. Assumed later. |
| **U** Undergraduate | The standard degree-level treatment, with proofs. |
| **A** Advanced | Graduate-level: the machinery needed for research. |
| **R** Research | Open problems, recent results, and where the machinery fails. |

</div>

A fresh undergraduate should read every **F** and **U** on a topic, then the
**A** sections of the topics they intend to specialise in. **R** sections assume
comfort with everything before them and are written to be read after the rest.

## 7. A practical schedule

The research above translates into a routine:

- **First pass.** Read the page. Attempt the recall prompts from memory. Read
  the worked examples actively, predicting each step.
- **Second pass, 1–2 days later.** Solve the completion problems without the
  notes. Anything you cannot do, mark.
- **Third pass, 1–2 weeks later.** Redo the marked problems *and two from an
  earlier topic*; that is the interleaving.
- **Before assessment.** Reconstruct the key definitions and theorem statements
  from memory, then check. Reconstructing a statement is harder and more useful
  than recognising it.

The second and third passes are where the learning happens. The first pass only
makes them possible.

## How To Use Learning Science
URL: https://mathematics.wyattau.com/how-to-use-learning-science/

<!-- Breadcrumb Schema for SEO -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [{"name": "Home", "url": "https://wyattau.com"}, {"name": "mathematics", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com"}, {"name": "mathematics", "url": "https://mathematics.wyattau.com/how-to-use-learning-science"}]
}
</script>

Reading is not learning. The six techniques on this page are the ones with the
strongest evidence from cognitive science; replicated across domains, age
groups, and decades. They are ranked by effect size from Dunlosky et al.
(2013), the most comprehensive review to date, and each is mapped to how the
notes on this site implement it.

The single most important finding: **the techniques that feel easiest are the
least effective, and the techniques that feel hardest are the most effective.**
Re-reading feels productive and produces almost no long-term retention.
Retrieval practice; actively pulling information from memory; feels harder
and produces dramatically better retention. The discomfort is the learning.

## Intuition

Think of memory as a muscle, not a container. You do not fill it by pouring
information in; you strengthen it by *retrieving* information out. Every time
you successfully recall a fact, the neural pathway gets stronger and the fact
becomes easier to recall next time. Every time you re-read a fact, you create
an *illusion of fluency*; the text looks familiar, so you think you know it,
but the retrieval pathway is unstrengthened and the fact will be gone in a
week.

This is why the notes have recall prompts at the top of every page (before you
read, try to recall what you already know) and self-tests at the end (after you
read, retrieve what you just learned). Both are retrieval practice, and both
are placed where the research says they belong: before (to activate prior
knowledge) and after (to consolidate).

## 1. Retrieval practice (the testing effect)

**The finding.** Actively recalling information from memory produces
substantially better long-term retention than re-reading the same information.
Roediger and Karpicke (2006) showed that students who tested themselves after
one reading retained 50% more after one week than students who re-read four
times; despite the re-readers feeling *more* confident.

**How this site implements it.** Every content page has **recall prompts** at
the top (attempt before reading; they activate prior knowledge and set the
retrieval framework) and **self-tests** at the bottom (attempt after reading -
they consolidate). The transition pages have six-question self-tests; the
graduate pages have interleaving problems; the ML course has code exercises
where you predict the output before running.

**How to use it.** After reading a section, close the page. Write down what you
remember. Open the page and check. The act of *trying* to recall; even when
you fail; strengthens the pathway more than re-reading does. This is the
hypercorrection effect: errors made during retrieval practice, when corrected,
produce better retention than correct answers on the first try.

**Citation.** Roediger, H.L. & Karpicke, J.D. (2006). "Test-enhanced learning:
Taking memory tests improves long-term retention." *Psychological Science*,
17(3), 249–255.

## 2. Spaced repetition

**The finding.** Information reviewed at *increasing intervals* is retained far
longer than information reviewed at fixed intervals or crammed. Ebbinghaus
(1885) discovered the forgetting curve; Cepeda et al. (2006) confirmed the
optimal spacing.

**How this site implements it.** The notes do not include a spaced-repetition
system (that requires a tool like Anki), but every page is *self-contained* -
you can return to it at any interval without needing the surrounding context.
The recall prompts at the top of each page are designed for a specific
spacing schedule: read today, attempt the recall prompts tomorrow, attempt
them again after one week, then after one month.

**How to use it.** Do not re-read the same page in the same session. Instead:
read page A, then page B, then return to page A's recall prompts. The
intervening material creates the spacing, and the return is harder (and more
effective) than immediate re-reading.

**Citation.** Cepeda, N.J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J.T., & Rohrer, D.
(2006). "Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative
synthesis." *Psychological Bulletin*, 132(3), 354–380.

## 3. Interleaving

**The finding.** Mixing different *types* of problems within a practice session
produces better learning than blocking by type; even though blocked practice
feels easier and produces better practice performance. Rohrer and Taylor (2007)
showed this for mathematics: students who practised in blocks (all volume, then
all surface area) felt more confident but scored worse than students who
practised interleaved.

**How this site implements it.** The problem sets at the end of each track mix
problem types. The self-tests on the transition pages mix logic, algebra,
geometry, and calculus. The recall prompts at the top of each page ask about
concepts from earlier tracks.

**How to use it.** Do not work through a track's problems in order without
revisiting earlier material. After finishing the measure-theory page, attempt a
problem from the topology page. The mixing forces you to *identify which
technique to use*; a skill that blocked practice never develops because the
technique is always the same as the previous problem.

**Citation.** Rohrer, D. & Taylor, K. (2007). "The shuffling of mathematics
problems improves learning." *Instructional Science*, 35, 481–498.

## 4. Worked examples

**The finding.** For novice learners, studying worked examples; complete
solutions shown step by step; produces better learning than solving equivalent
problems, because solving requires the student to hold both the problem's
structure and the solution procedure in working memory simultaneously, which
overloads a novice's capacity. Sweller and Cooper (1985) called this the
**worked-example effect** and grounded it in **cognitive load theory**.

**How this site implements it.** Every proof page has worked examples with
every step shown. The measure-theory page's Stokes' theorem proof shows every
sign's origin. The functional analysis page's Hahn–Banach proof shows the
one-dimensional extension, then the Zorn's lemma step, with each
sub-derivation explicit.

**How to use it.** For novices: read the worked example first. Cover the
solution. Attempt the same problem. Uncover and compare. The key is the
*comparison*; what did you miss? For intermediates: attempt the problem first,
then read the worked example and identify the differences. The progression from
worked example to faded guidance to independent solving is called scaffolding.

**Citation.** Sweller, J. & Cooper, G.A. (1985). "The use of worked examples as
a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra." *Cognition and
Instruction*, 2(1), 59–89.

## 5. Elaboration

**The finding.** Connecting new information to existing knowledge; asking
"why?", generating examples, explaining in your own words; produces deeper
understanding and better retention than passive reading. Dunlosky et al. (2013)
rated self-explanation as "moderate utility" and elaborative interrogation as
promising.

**How this site implements it.** Every content page has an **Intuition**
section before the formal definitions, and every proof page has a section that
names *where each hypothesis is spent*. The intuition section is the
elaboration: it connects the formal statement to something you already
understand. The "where each hypothesis is spent" section is self-explanation:
it forces you to see *why* the condition is needed, not just that it is listed.

**How to use it.** After reading a theorem, close the page and try to explain
why the theorem is true in your own words; without the proof. Then read the
proof and compare. The gap between your explanation and the proof is where
your understanding is incomplete.

## 6. Dual coding

**The finding.** Information presented in both verbal and visual formats is
remembered better than either alone, because the two channels are processed by
different cognitive systems and create independent memory traces (Paivio,
1971).

**How this site implements it.** Every major concept has both a verbal
description and a visual or diagrammatic representation. The topology page's
continuity section has both the epsilon-delta definition and the intuitive
description. The ML course's code examples produce visual output (plots,
printed values) alongside the mathematical statements.

## 7. What does NOT work

**Re-reading.** The most common study technique produces almost no long-term
retention. The illusion of fluency; "I recognise this text"; is mistaken for
knowledge. Dunlosky et al. rated it "low utility."

**Highlighting.** The second most common technique performs no better than
reading, because it requires no active processing. Highlighting selects
information but does not require retrieval or elaboration.

**Cramming.** Massed practice produces good short-term performance and poor
long-term retention, exactly as the spacing effect predicts. The crammer's
exam score will be higher than the spacer's the next day, but the spacer's
score one month later will be dramatically higher.

**Passive video watching.** Watching someone else solve problems does not
build the retrieval pathways that solving them yourself does. Videos are
useful for *initial exposure*; seeing the technique demonstrated; but the
learning happens when you attempt the problem yourself.

## 8. The meta-lesson

Every technique that works requires *effort during learning*. The effort is
the signal that the retrieval pathway is being strengthened. If studying feels
easy, you are not learning; you are performing the illusion of learning. The
harder the retrieval, the stronger the retention.

This is Dunlosky et al.'s most important finding: the techniques students
report using most (re-reading, highlighting) are the ones with the least
evidence, and the techniques with the most evidence (practice testing,
distributed practice) are the ones students report using least. The reason is
that effective techniques feel harder, and students mistake difficulty for
ineffectiveness.

These notes are designed to make the effective techniques easier to use -
recall prompts at the right moments, self-tests at the right intervals,
worked examples at the right depth; but the effort must come from you.

## Why This Guide Exists

University mathematics is fundamentally different from computational mathematics. It asks not "what is the answer?" but "why must this be true, and what would have to change for it to be false?" This shift, from computation to proof, is what transforms a collection of facts into genuine mathematical understanding.

Work through the Mathematics sections in order, starting with Abstract Algebra and Complex Analysis and building toward Abstract Algebra, Complex Analysis, Demos, Diagnostics, Differential Geometry, Functional Analysis, Linear Algebra, Measure Theory, Multivariable Calculus, Number Theory, Ordinary Differential Equations, Probability And Statistics, Real Analysis, Topology and Zh, then check yourself with the practice problems for each topic. The prerequisite map shows you exactly how the subjects connect, so you can study in the right order and build understanding that compounds. Each section includes definitions, theorems, worked examples, common pitfalls, and practice problems.

## Abstract Algebra

Abstract algebra studies algebraic structures, groups, rings, fields, and their homomorphisms. It reveals the architecture of mathematical objects by focusing on their symmetries and operations rather than their specific elements.

### Core Topics

- [Groups](/1-abstract-algebra/1_groups/), definition, examples, and basic properties
- [Subgroups](/1-abstract-algebra/2_subgroups/), criteria for subgroups and lattice of subgroups
- [Lagrange's Theorem](/1-abstract-algebra/3_lagrange-s-theorem/), the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group
- [Normal Subgroups and Quotient Groups](/1-abstract-algebra/4_normal-subgroups-and-quotient-groups/), when subgroups are "invisible" to the group structure
- [Homomorphisms and Isomorphism Theorems](/1-abstract-algebra/5_homomorphisms-and-isomorphism-theorems/), the structural maps between groups
- [Group Actions](/1-abstract-algebra/6_group-actions/), how groups act on sets: orbits, stabilisers, and Burnside's lemma
- [The Sylow Theorems](/1-abstract-algebra/7_the-sylow-theorems/), existence and conjugacy of p-subgroups
- [Rings](/1-abstract-algebra/8_rings/), ring axioms, ideals, and ring homomorphisms
- [Ideals and Quotient Rings](/1-abstract-algebra/9_ideals-and-quotient-rings/), building new rings from old
- [Polynomial Rings](/1-abstract-algebra/10_polynomial-rings/), Euclidean algorithm and factorisation
- [Euclidean Domains, PIDs, and UFDs](/1-abstract-algebra/11_euclidean-domains-pids-and-ufds/), the hierarchy of ring types
- [Field Theory](/1-abstract-algebra/12_field-theory/), field extensions and algebraic numbers
- [Galois Theory Fundamentals](/1-abstract-algebra/13_galois-theory-fundamentals/), the connection between field extensions and group theory
- [Classification of Groups of Small Order](/1-abstract-algebra/16_classification-of-groups-of-small-order/)

## Linear Algebra

Linear algebra is the most widely applied area of mathematics. It handles vector spaces, linear maps, eigenvalues, and inner product spaces, tools used in data science, quantum mechanics, computer graphics, and virtually every branch of applied mathematics.

### Core Topics

- [Vectors and Vector Spaces](/2-linear-algebra/1_vectors-and-vector-spaces/), axioms, examples, and subspaces
- [Linear Independence, Span, Basis, and Dimension](/2-linear-algebra/2_linear-independence-span-basis-and-dimension/), the fundamental structural concepts
- [Matrices](/2-linear-algebra/3_matrices/), matrix operations, inverse, and rank
- [Systems of Linear Equations](/2-linear-algebra/4_systems-of-linear-equations/), Gaussian elimination and row echelon form
- [Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](/2-linear-algebra/5_eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors/), diagonalisation and the characteristic polynomial
- [Inner Product Spaces](/2-linear-algebra/7_inner-product-spaces/), orthogonality, Gram-Schmidt, and projections
- [Singular Value Decomposition](/2-linear-algebra/8_singular-value-decomposition/), the most important factorisation in applied mathematics

### Problem Set

- [Problem Set](/2-linear-algebra/9_problem-set/)

## Real Analysis

Real analysis provides the rigorous foundation for calculus. The ε-δ framework formalises limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration on the real line. This is where you learn to prove the theorems that calculus takes for granted.

### Core Topics

- [The Real Number System](/3-real-analysis/1_the-real-number-system/), completeness, Archimedean property, and density of rationals
- [Sequences and Limits](/3-real-analysis/2_sequences-and-limits/), convergence, bounded sequences, and monotone convergence
- [Series](/3-real-analysis/3_series/), convergence tests, absolute vs conditional convergence, and rearrangements
- [Continuity](/3-real-analysis/4_continuity/), ε-δ definition, uniform continuity, and the intermediate value theorem
- [Differentiability](/3-real-analysis/5_differentiability/), the derivative as a limit, mean value theorem, and L'Hôpital's rule
- [Riemann Integration](/3-real-analysis/6_riemann-integration/), Riemann sums, integrability conditions, and the fundamental theorem
- [Sequences and Series of Functions](/3-real-analysis/7_sequences-and-series-of-functions/), pointwise vs uniform convergence, power series, and Weierstrass M-test

### Problem Set

- [Problem Set](/3-real-analysis/8_problem-set/)

## Multivariable Calculus

Multivariable calculus extends single-variable calculus to functions of several variables. Partial derivatives, multiple integrals, and vector calculus theorems (Green's, Stokes', and Gauss') provide the mathematical tools for physics and engineering.

### Core Topics

- [Partial Derivatives](/4-multivariable-calculus/1_partial-derivatives/), gradients, directional derivatives, and the chain rule
- [Multiple Integrals](/4-multivariable-calculus/2_multiple-integrals/), double and triple integrals, change of variables, and Jacobians
- [Vector Calculus](/4-multivariable-calculus/3_vector-calculus/), gradient, divergence, curl, and their identities
- [Optimisation](/4-multivariable-calculus/4_optimization/), critical points, Hessian matrix, and Lagrange multipliers
- [Curves and Surfaces](/4-multivariable-calculus/5_curves-and-surfaces/), parameterised curves, tangent spaces, and surface integrals

### Problem Set

## Ordinary Differential Equations

ODEs describe how quantities change in relation to each other, the language of dynamical systems, population models, electrical circuits, and mechanical vibrations. The course covers solution techniques, stability analysis, and an introduction to partial differential equations.

### Core Topics

- [Introduction and Classification](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/1_introduction-and-classification/), order, linearity, and initial/boundary value problems
- [First-Order ODEs](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/2_first-order-odes/), separable, exact, and integrating factor methods
- Higher-Order Linear ODEs, characteristic equation, undetermined coefficients, and variation of parameters
- [Laplace Transforms](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/5_laplace-transforms/), transforming ODEs into algebraic equations
- [Series Solutions](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/6_series-solutions/), power series methods and Frobenius method
- [Fourier Series](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/7_fourier-series/), representing periodic functions as sums of sines and cosines
- [Introduction to PDEs](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/8_introduction-to-partial-differential-equations/), heat equation, wave equation, and Laplace's equation
- [Stability and Phase Plane Analysis](/5-ordinary-differential-equations/9_stability-and-phase-plane-analysis/), equilibrium points, linearisation, and bifurcations

## Complex Analysis

Complex analysis studies functions of a complex variable. The central result, differentiability once implies infinite differentiability, makes complex analysis the most elegant branch of analysis. It provides powerful tools for evaluating real integrals and understanding analytic continuation.

### Core Topics

- [Complex Numbers Review](/6-complex-analysis/1_complex-numbers-review/), algebra, geometry, and polar form
- [Complex Functions and Analyticity](/6-complex-analysis/2_complex-functions-and-analyticity/), the Cauchy-Riemann equations and analytic functions
- [The Cauchy-Riemann Equations](/6-complex-analysis/3_the-cauchy-riemann-equations/), necessary and sufficient conditions for analyticity
- [Complex Integration](/6-complex-analysis/4_complex-integration/), contour integrals and path independence
- [Cauchy's Theorem](/6-complex-analysis/5_cauchy-s-theorem/), the central result: the integral of an analytic function over a closed contour is zero
- [Cauchy's Integral Formula](/6-complex-analysis/6_cauchy-s-integral-formula/), recovering function values from boundary integrals
- [Taylor and Laurent Series](/6-complex-analysis/7_taylor-and-laurent-series/), series expansions of analytic functions
- [Singularities and Residue Theory](/6-complex-analysis/8_singularities-and-residue-theory/), classifying singularities and computing residues
- [Applications of Contour Integration](/6-complex-analysis/9_applications-of-contour-integration/), evaluating real integrals using complex methods
- [Conformal Mappings](/6-complex-analysis/10_conformal-mappings/), angle-preserving maps and their applications
- [Liouville's Theorem and the Maximum Modulus Principle](/6-complex-analysis/11_liouville-s-theorem-and-the-maximum-modulus-principle/)
- [Argument Principle and Rouché's Theorem](/6-complex-analysis/12_argument-principle-and-rouch-s-theorem/)
- [Analytic Continuation](/6-complex-analysis/13_analytic-continuation/)

## Number Theory

Number theory studies the properties of integers, divisibility, primes, congruences, and Diophantine equations. It is both one of the oldest branches of mathematics and one with profound modern applications in cryptography and coding theory.

- [Number Theory](/7-number-theory/), Euclidean algorithm, fundamental theorem of arithmetic, modular arithmetic, Fermat's little theorem, and Euler's theorem

## Probability and Statistics

Probability theory provides the mathematical framework for uncertainty. Starting from axiomatic probability, it builds through random variables, distributions, and limit theorems to the measure-theoretic foundations used in modern statistics and stochastic processes.

### Core Topics

- [Probability Spaces](/8-probability-and-statistics/1_probability-spaces/), sample spaces, events, and the axioms of probability
- [Random Variables](/8-probability-and-statistics/2_random-variables/), discrete and continuous random variables, PMFs, PDFs, and CDFs
- [Joint Distributions and Independence](/8-probability-and-statistics/3_joint-distributions-and-independence/), marginal and conditional distributions, covariance, and correlation
- [Limit Theorems](/8-probability-and-statistics/4_limit-theorems/), law of large numbers and central limit theorem
- [Transformations and Convolutions](/8-probability-and-statistics/5_transformations-and-convolutions/), changing variables and adding random variables
- [Probability and Statistics](/8-probability-and-statistics/6_probability-and-statistics/), the combined probability and statistics reference
- [Estimation and Hypothesis Testing](/8-probability-and-statistics/7_estimation-and-hypothesis-testing/), maximum likelihood, the Cramer-Rao bound, the Neyman-Pearson lemma, p-values and the standard tests

## Topology

Topology generalises continuity and convergence beyond metric spaces. It studies the properties of spaces that are preserved under continuous deformations, connectivity, compactness, and the fundamental group. Topology is the language of modern geometry and analysis.

### Core Topics

- [Introduction to Topology](/9-topology/1_introduction-to-topology/), motivation, examples, and topological equivalence
- [Topological Spaces](/9-topology/2_topological-spaces/), open sets, bases, and subbases
- [Closed Sets, Closure, Interior, and Boundary](/9-topology/3_closed-sets-closure-interior-and-boundary/)
- [Continuity and Homeomorphisms](/9-topology/4_continuity-and-homeomorphisms/), the topological notion of continuity
- [Compactness](/9-topology/5_compactness/), the topological analogue of finiteness
- [Connectedness](/9-topology/6_connectedness/), path-connected and simply connected spaces
- [Metric Spaces](/9-topology/7_metric-spaces/), metrics as a special case of topology
- [Separation Axioms](/9-topology/8_separation-axioms/), T₀, T₁, T₂, and Hausdorff spaces
- [Introduction to Algebraic Topology](/9-topology/9_introduction-to-algebraic-topology/), fundamental group and homotopy

## Measure Theory

Measure theory extends integration beyond the Riemann integral. The Lebesgue integral handles a far wider class of functions and provides the rigorous foundation for probability theory, Fourier analysis, and functional analysis.

- [Measurable Functions](/10-measure-theory/5_measurable-functions/), the measurability analogue of continuity
- [Lebesgue Integration](/10-measure-theory/6_lebesgue-integration/), building integrals with measure theory

Functional analysis extends linear algebra to infinite-dimensional vector spaces, function spaces. It provides the mathematical framework for quantum mechanics, partial differential equations, and signal processing.

## Proof Techniques

Proof-based mathematics requires mastery of several proof strategies. Knowing which technique to reach for is the core skill of mathematical reasoning.

<div class="table-wrap">

| Technique | When to Use | Example |
| ----------- | ------------- | --------- |
| Direct proof | Implication P ⇒ Q | "If n is even, then n² is even" |
| Contrapositive | Easier to prove ¬Q ⇒ ¬P | "If n² is odd, then n is odd" |
| Contradiction | Assume ¬P, derive contradiction | Irrationality of √2 |
| Induction | Statement about natural numbers | Σi = n(n+1)/2 |
| Construction | Existence proof | "There exist infinitely many primes" |
| Case analysis | Statement splits into cases | "Every integer is even or odd" |

</div>

### Tips for Writing Proofs

1. **State what you are proving clearly**, rephrase the theorem in your own words
2. **Identify the hypothesis and conclusion**, know what you are given and what you must show
3. **Work backwards from the conclusion**, what would you need to prove the final statement?
4. **Use definitions**, every proof starts with what you know by definition
5. **Be precise**, every step must follow logically from the previous one
6. **Check edge cases**, does the proof work for n = 0, n = 1, negative numbers, etc.?

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Where should I start?

If you are new to proof-based mathematics, start with [Linear Algebra](/2-linear-algebra/), it is the most broadly applicable and has the gentlest learning curve. If you are already comfortable with proofs, start with [Real Analysis](/3-real-analysis/) for the foundations of rigorous calculus, or [Abstract Algebra](/1-abstract-algebra/) for algebraic structures.

### How long does each subject take?

Each subject requires approximately 6–8 weeks of focused study at a university pace. This means reading the notes, working through the examples, and completing the problem sets. Do not rush, mathematics is cumulative, and weak foundations create problems later.

### Are these notes suitable for self-study?

Yes. Each section includes definitions, theorems, proofs, worked examples, and common pitfalls. Work through the examples with paper and pen, do not just read them. Then attempt the problem sets to test your understanding.

### What is the difference between these notes and a textbook?

These notes follow the standard university curriculum and cover the same material as textbooks like Artin (Algebra), Rudin (Analysis), or Axler (Linear Algebra). They are designed as a complement to, not a replacement for, a full textbook. Use them for quick reference, review, and additional examples.

### How do I get better at proofs?

Practice. Read proofs in the notes, then try to reproduce them from memory. Attempt the problem sets without looking at solutions. Discuss proofs with other students. The ability to write proofs develops through active practice, not passive reading.

### Do I need all these subjects?

It depends on your goals. If you are studying physics, you need linear algebra, ODEs, real analysis, complex analysis, and differential geometry. If you are studying computer science, you need linear algebra, probability, and discrete mathematics (covered in ODEs). If you are studying pure mathematics, you need all of them.

## Why a course on this site at all

Because the encyclopaedia's strengths are the course's weaknesses. An
encyclopaedia lets you look up the mean value theorem; it cannot tell you
what you needed to read first. A course gives you the order and refuses
to let a chapter assume anything you have not met. The Core Course on
this site is the second kind of object: one sequence, dependency-ordered,
with every prerequisite machine-checked before anything ships. You do not
browse it. You walk it.

## The encyclopaedia: what you will find

The reference tracks cover the undergraduate canon and part of the
graduate shelves, proof-based throughout:

- **Abstract Algebra**: groups, rings, and fields, from cyclic groups to
  Galois theory.
- **Real Analysis**: limits, continuity, and the ε-δ framework.
- **Linear Algebra**: vector spaces, eigenvalues, inner product spaces.
- **Multivariable Calculus**: gradient, multiple integrals, and the
  theorems of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
- **Complex Analysis**: analytic functions, contour integration, residues.
- **Differential Geometry**: manifolds, curvature, geometric structures.
- **Functional Analysis**: infinite-dimensional spaces and bounded
  operators; the mathematics behind quantum mechanics and PDE theory.
- **Measure Theory, Probability, Topology, Number Theory**: the measure-
  theoretic foundations, the distributions, the qualitative geometry, and
  the arithmetic of the integers.

Every track carries worked examples, common mistakes, and practice
problems with spaced-repetition review.

## Common Mistakes

**Confusing proof-based mathematics with computational mathematics:**
these notes emphasise rigorous proofs and definitions, not formulas and
techniques. A correct answer without a valid proof is insufficient.

**Skipping prerequisite topics:** mathematics is cumulative, and skipping
foundations compounds gaps. This is precisely why the course exists: its
order is checked so that skipping is a choice you cannot make by
accident.

**Treating definitions as interchangeable across fields:** the word
"normal" means different things in group theory, linear algebra, and
topology. Always check which definition applies in the current context.

## Mathematics

Welcome to the mathematics notes. These notes cover proof-based undergraduate mathematics, from foundational algebraic structures to advanced analysis and geometry.

## Why This Matters

Mathematics is the language of science and engineering. Abstract algebra provides the algebraic foundations (groups, rings, fields), real analysis builds rigorous calculus, linear algebra handles vector spaces and transformations, and topology generalises continuity and convergence. These subjects interconnect deeply, linear algebra appears in functional analysis, group theory underpins symmetry in physics, and measure theory extends integration beyond Riemann's limitations. Understanding these connections is what transforms computation into understanding.

## What You Will Find

- **Abstract Algebra**: Groups, rings, fields, and their homomorphisms, the algebraic structures underlying symmetry and number theory. From the cyclic group ℤ/nℤ to the Monster group, abstract algebra reveals the architecture of mathematical objects.
- **Real Analysis**: Rigorous treatment of limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration on the real line. The ε-δ framework provides the logical foundation for all of calculus.
- **Linear Algebra**: Vector spaces, linear maps, eigenvalues, and inner product spaces. Linear algebra is the most widely applied area of mathematics, from data science to quantum mechanics.
- **Multivariable Calculus**: Partial derivatives, gradient, multiple integrals, and vector calculus theorems. Green's, Stokes', and Gauss' theorems unify differential and integral calculus.
- **Complex Analysis**: Analytic functions, contour integration, and the residue theorem. Complex analysis is the most elegant branch of analysis, differentiability once implies infinite differentiability.
- **Differential Geometry**: Manifolds, curvature, and geometric structures on smooth spaces. Differential geometry connects calculus to geometry, enabling the study of curved spaces.
- **Functional Analysis**: Infinite-dimensional vector spaces, bounded operators, and spectral theory. Functional analysis extends linear algebra to function spaces, underpinning quantum mechanics and PDE theory.

## Core Concepts

<div class="table-wrap">

| Area | Central Object | Key Result | Application |
| ------ | --------------- | ------------ | ------------- |
| Abstract Algebra | Group $(G, \cdot)$ | Lagrange's Theorem | Symmetry, cryptography |
| Real Analysis | $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit | Bolzano-Weierstrass | Rigorous calculus |
| Linear Algebra | Vector space $V$ | Spectral Theorem | Data science, quantum |
| Complex Analysis | Analytic function $f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ | Cauchy's Integral Theorem | Contour integration |
| Differential Geometry | Smooth manifold $M$ | Gauss-Bonnet Theorem | General relativity |
| Functional Analysis | Banach/Hilbert space | Hahn-Banach Theorem | PDE theory, quantum |

</div>

## Proof Techniques

<div class="table-wrap">

| Technique | When to Use | Example |
| ----------- | ------------- | --------- |
| Direct proof | Implication $P \Rightarrow Q$ | "If $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is even" |
| Contrapositive | Easier to prove $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ | "If $n^2$ is odd, then $n$ is odd" |
| Contradiction | Assume $\neg P$, derive contradiction | Irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ |
| Induction | Statement about natural numbers | $\sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ |
| Construction | Existence proof | "There exist infinitely many primes" |

</div>

Mathematics is cumulative, each topic builds on previous ones. If you encounter unfamiliar material, check the prerequisites and review foundational concepts first.

- [Classical Mechanics](https://physics.wyattau.com/1-classical-mechanics/)
- [Electromagnetism](https://physics.wyattau.com/3-electromagnetism/)

## Common Mistakes

**Assuming mathematics is about memorising formulas:** These notes are proof-based, understanding why a theorem is true matters more than knowing the statement. Memorising the spectral theorem without understanding its proof leaves you unable to apply it in novel situations.

**Confusing "obvious" with "proven":** In proof-based mathematics, intuition can be misleading. The statement "every continuous function is differentiable" seems plausible until you encounter the Weierstrass function. Always write out the full proof rather than relying on intuition alone.

**Neglecting the role of counterexamples:** A single counterexample disproves a universal claim. Knowing classic counterexamples (the topologist's sine curve, the Cantor set, pathological algebraic structures) is as important as knowing theorems. They sharpen your understanding of where definitions and theorems apply.

## Intuition

Mathematics is not about memorising formulas or computing answers, it's about building a network of ideas that connect to each other in logically airtight ways. The reason proof-based mathematics feels fundamentally different from computational mathematics is that it's asking a different question. Computational maths asks "what is the answer?" Proof-based maths asks "why must this be true, and what would have to change for it to be false?" This shift in perspective is what transforms a collection of facts into genuine understanding. When you prove a theorem, you're not just verifying a result, you're building a bridge between what you already know and something new, and that bridge must hold weight from every possible direction.

The interconnectedness of mathematical subjects is not a coincidence, it reflects deep structural parallels. Groups describe symmetry, vector spaces describe linear structure, topological spaces describe continuity, and measure spaces describe size. These aren't separate topics; they're different lenses on the same fundamental questions about mathematical objects and their relationships. Understanding why the spectral theorem matters in linear algebra, why compactness matters in analysis, and why the isomorphism theorems matter in algebra, and how they all connect, is what transforms computation into mathematical maturity.

The proof techniques themselves are not arbitrary logical exercises. Direct proof builds a chain from assumptions to conclusion. Proof by contradiction exploits the fact that if a statement isn't true, assuming it's true must create a logical impossibility. Induction captures the idea that if something holds for a base case and each step preserves it, it holds for all natural numbers. Each technique is a tool for attacking a different kind of problem, and learning to recognise which technique to reach for is the core skill of mathematical reasoning.

## Mathematics

This section presents proof-based undergraduate mathematics at the rigour
expected of a university programme. The treatment emphasises precise
definitions, complete proofs, and the logical dependencies between topics: each
subject begins with its axioms and builds upward, so that no result is invoked
before it has been established.

The material spans the core analytical and algebraic strands. Real analysis
reconstructs the calculus from the topology of the real line; linear algebra
treats vector spaces and linear maps in full generality; multivariable calculus
extends differentiation and integration to functions of several variables.
Where a result admits multiple proofs, the most instructive is given; where a
computation is required, every step is shown.

Readers should be comfortable with single-variable calculus and with reading
and constructing proofs. Cross-references link related results across subjects.

## Intuition

Mathematics is the art of precise abstraction. Each subject in this collection strips away the inessential to reveal underlying structure: analysis formalises limits and continuity, algebra captures symmetry and arithmetic, and geometry studies shape and curvature. The power of mathematics lies in its cumulative nature: theorems proven once are true forever, and each result becomes a tool for the next. Learning mathematics is less about memorising formulas and more about internalising ways of thinking: decomposing problems, identifying invariants, and translating between different representations of the same structure.

## Common Mistakes

**Mistake 1: Skipping foundational topics to jump to advanced material**
Students often attempt measure theory or algebraic topology without a solid grasp of real analysis and linear algebra. This leads to shallow understanding and an inability to construct proofs. Master the foundational subjects first, as the later material builds directly on them.

**Mistake 2: Reading proofs without attempting to reconstruct them**
Mathematics is learned by doing, not by passive reading. Directly following a proof step-by-step gives a false sense of comprehension. After reading a proof, close the book and try to reproduce it from memory, filling in gaps by working through the logical structure yourself.

**Mistake 3: Treating definitions as suggestions rather than precise requirements**
In proof-based mathematics, every word in a definition matters. For example, a "normal subgroup" requires both closure under conjugation and the subgroup property. Omitting any condition leads to incorrect results. Always verify that all parts of a definition are satisfied before applying a theorem.
